#8921. International photography museum Fotografiska opens in Shenzhen

Fotografiska Shenzhen is located in Shenzhen Bay MixC, an upscale retail and culture complex © SFAP Architectural Photography

The international photography museum Fotografiska has recently launched in Shenzhen, its second space in mainland China, after Fotografiska Shanghai opened in 2023. “The strategy was always to self-fund the first space in Shanghai, and then expand through strategic partnerships for subsequent locations,” says Christian Devillers, the managing director for Fotografiska China.

The organisation, founded in Stockholm in 2010, also currently has locations in the Swedish capital, New York, Berlin and Tallinn; and a new venue, in Oslo, is scheduled to open in 2028.

“Museum-going culture [in Shenzhen] isn’t as deeply entrenched as it is in Shanghai or Hong Kong,” Devillers says, and its art-going demographic skews heavily toward young families and professionals. Fotografiska Shenzhen is replicating Shanghai’s late hours and lifestyle offerings, which draw office workers commuting to the city centres, and its first public day on the 1 October national holiday drew more than 1,000 paying visitors.

The project opened with exhibitions across the 5,300 sq. m facility, including a Shi Guowei solo show and Toiletpaper, showcasing Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari’s titular magazine (both until 14 March 2027). They have joined a show of photography award Prix Pictet (until 29 November), the six-artist group show Transcendent Realities (until 1 October 2027) and a Michael Najjar solo exhibition (until 17 January 2027). Subsequent planned events include a show of Hong Kong photographers featuring, among others, Ho Fan (1931-2016).

In Shanghai, even with Fotografiska’s busy traffic, admissions and memberships account for only around 20% of total revenue, Devillers says. The museum instead depends on commercial partnerships, and retail and food and drink sales. Fotografiska Shenzhen’s six-year partnership agreement with landlord China Resources Land aims to draw a profit by year three. The institution has set an initial target of 70,000 visitors for 2027.

Fotografiska Shenzhen is located in the upscale retail complex Shenzhen Bay MixC, which is also home to a new immersive art concept called Base. They join several new and forthcoming cultural projects in the city, which is making a concerted push to raise its artistic profile, such as the recently-opened Shenzhen International Art Museum and Shenzhen Bay Cultural Plaza. This month will also see the long-running Hong Kong fair Fine Art Asia relocate to the mainland city (26-29 November).

#8919. Photographer’s Camera Plunges 150 Feet Off a Cliff After Tripod Mishap

Photographer’s Camera Plunges 150 Feet Off a Cliff After Tripod Mishap

A photographer didn’t expect to see her camera again after it plunged 150 feet off a cliff in Arkansas — until a well-known photographer stepped in.

KY3 reports that on November 19, Heinrichs was hiking on Hawksbill Crag in the Upper Buffalo Wilderness.

Hawksbill Crag is a magnet for photographers thanks to the unusual way it juts out over the oak-hickory forest.

Heinrichs was doing just that, taking photos near Hawksbill Crag with her Nikon D750 mounted on a tripod.

“I turned around for maybe five seconds or so and turned back around to my camera and I saw it falling off the side of a cliff,” Heinrichs tells KY3. “About 150 feet down.”

The problem? One of the tripod legs wasn’t locked properly, causing it to fall over. This is normally bad enough without the camera going over a huge cliff.

“It was heartbreaking,” adds Heinrichs. “I could just feel my heart sink and drop when it happened.”

The photographer turned to a local Facebook page, Our Buffalo River, explaining that she “had a camera mishap” and that her D750 was now at the bottom of Hawksbill Crag.

Tim Ernst, a wilderness and nature photographer who is based in northern Arkansas, saw the post and responded.

“Hey, I got an excuse to run out to the Crag,” Ernst tells KY3. “So that was an easy call on my part. I literally jumped up and took off and headed to the Crag.”

And it turns out that Heinrichs is a fan of Ernst, who is a well-established photographer whose work has appeared in National Geographic and the New York Times.

“I’ve followed Tim Ernst for years,” says Heinrichs. “And so for him to be the one to reach out and do that it, I was starstruck a little bit.”

Ernst found the camera sitting on a pile of leaves. However, it wasn’t in great shape.

“I immediately knew it was not good because the lens that was on it had actually separated,” says Ernst.

It appears the camera is beyond repair, but Heinrichs says she’s grateful to Ernst for reaching out and trying. She does plan to replace the camera.

#8917. Melania Trump Is Selling $150 Digital Photos of Herself Taken by Ellen von Unwerth

Melania Trump Is Selling $150 Digital Photos of Herself Taken by Ellen von Unwerth

U.S. first lady Melania Trump is selling digital photos of herself shot by influential fashion photographer Ellen von Unwerth for $150.

Melania made the announcement of the sale of “exclusive” photographs taken by von Unwerth in a post on X (the platform formerly known as Twitter) on Sunday. The launch coincides with the release of MELANIA: The Series, a new two-part production focusing on the wife of President Donald Trump, which debuted on Amazon Prime Video on November 20.

— MELANIA TRUMP (@MELANIATRUMP) November 22, 2026

According to the product listing on Melania’s official website for the “PhotoArchival Digital Edition”, she collaborated with von Unwerth over a two-day photo shoot “to develop the visual narrative” of the images. The photographs are being sold for $150 as a digital album delivered in the form of a movie file.

According to a report by Newsweek, buyers are also required to have a cryptocurrency wallet on the Solana blockchain to store the digital collectible. While customers can currently pay by credit card, they must connect their cryptocurrency wallet to Melania’s website before completing the purchase.

“Melania Trump is launching PhotoArchival Digital Edition, an exclusive collection of digital photographs by internationally acclaimed fashion photographer Ellen von Unwerth,” the announcement on X states. “The collection presents a visual portrait of Mrs. Trump, showcasing von Unwerth’s distinctive artistry. Its release coincides with the debut of MELANIA, The Series, a new two-part production streaming on Amazon Prime Video.”

Von Unwerth also shot the photography for Melania, the documentary about the first lady released in January, and some of the images featured in the $150 PhotoArchival Digital Edition appear to be the same. One of von Unwerth’s black-and-white photographs shows Melania wearing a fitted suit, sitting in a chair with her legs crossed and looking directly at the camera. Another image shows Melania standing beside a mirror in a strapless black dress as someone holds a clapperboard in the shot.

The release of Melania’s digital photo collection follows a recent interview in which von Unwerth, one of the most sought-after fashion photographers working today, claimed that “there’s no money left” in the industry.

#8915. Getty Images Demands Release of Veteran Photographer Detained in Iran

Getty Images Demands Release of Veteran Photographer Detained in Iran

Getty Images is demanding the release of veteran Iranian photojournalist Majid Saeedi, a regular contributor to the photo agency who has been detained in Iran for more than two months.

Saeedi is an internationally recognized photojournalist who has won numerous awards for his coverage of Afghanistan, including a Lucie Award and the Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award. His images have been published in The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Life magazine. Saeedi also received second prize in the 2013 World Press Photo Contest’s Contemporary Issues category.

According to a report by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), Saeedi was arrested at his home in Tehran on September 9. More than two months after his arrest, Iranian authorities have yet to disclose whether the freelance photojournalist faces any charges or which agency is holding him, despite repeated efforts to obtain this information. Saeedi is believed to be detained in Kerman, a city in southeastern Iran, although his location has not been officially confirmed.

The CPJ and Getty Images have now urged Iranian authorities to release the award-winning photojournalist immediately and unconditionally. They say that the lack of information surrounding his detention has raised serious concerns about his safety, as well as the increasing threats facing independent journalists in Iran.

“Holding Majid Saeedi for more than two months, with no official confirmation of any charges, is unacceptable,” Getty Images VP of Global News Pancho Bernasconi says. “Journalism is not a crime. We join CPJ in demanding Iranian authorities account for Majid’s whereabouts and release him immediately and unconditionally.”

“For more than two months, Majid Saeedi’s family has been left in the dark about his whereabouts, the reason for his detention, and whether he is safe. No journalist should simply disappear into state custody, while Iranian authorities refuse to tell their family what has happened,” CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah says in a further statement. “Majid’s detention is part of a broader campaign to intimidate and silence journalists in Iran — he must be released immediately and unconditionally.

Saeedi has previously been arrested on several occasions in connection with his photographic coverage of politically sensitive events and their aftermath, including in 2009, 2021, and June 2025. According to CPJ, the photographer’s latest detention comes amid an escalating crackdown on independent journalism in Iran, where authorities have increasingly resorted to arrests and lengthy prison sentences to suppress critical reporting.

Previously, PetaPixel reported on two female photographers, prominent photojournalist Yalda Moaiery and 18-year-old artist Shaghayegh Afshar, who were sentenced to a combined 24 years in prison in Iran. Meanwhile Tahmineh Monzavi, an acclaimed Iranian documentary photographer, was sentenced to 74 lashes for documenting an Iranian female singer’s concert.

#8913. ‘I want the experiences I had to be available forever’: arts figures and scientists hit out at proposed job cuts at Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery

TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium

More than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution. The signatories include the former Tasmanian premier Lara Giddings and the 2014 Man Booker Prize winner Richard Flanagan, along with 44 leading-scientists representing universities in the UK, Europe, Canada, USA, Russia and Australia.

TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium. Its “science collections are really critical on a global scale for research around climate change and species extinction,” explains Ian Terry, the chair of Friends of TMAG and the museum’s former senior curator of cultural heritage (2006-2017).

Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.

Staff at the TMAG were briefed in August that up to 19.7 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs, or roughly 30% of its workforce would be axed to rein in government spending. The government has disputed the claim that the scale of the required cuts has been confirmed; a spokesperson is quoted in ABC News as saying “TMAG is not required to reduce its workforce by 30%”.

However, since news of cuts were made public Tasmanian MPs, TMAG’s executive and its board have received more than 25 letters from prominent European scientists that have decried the government’s planned cuts, and warned its decision to axe the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium, Gintaras Kantvilas, an internationally renowned biologist, would have “consequences far beyond Tasmania”.

This week’s letter called for the Tasmanian government to recognise its “statutory obligation to care for approximately one million objects of inestimable value” and “reconsider the proposed job cuts with their unintended deleterious consequences on the Tasmanian economy.”

“I want TMAG properly funded. I want the life-changing childhood experiences I had at TMAG to be available to all Tasmanians forever,” David Walsh, the founder of Hobart’s Museum of Old and New Art (MONA), and one of the letter’s signatories, wrote in a separate letter that was published in Hobart’s Mercury newspaper this week. “I put stuff on Mona’s wall because TMAG put stuff in my heart,” he added.

The proposed job losses are part of wide-ranging cost cutting initiatives being rolled out by the state Liberal government, as part of an attempt to rein in the state’s ballooning debt, which is projected to reach A$9.9bn (£5bn) by 2027-28. These initiatives include a plan to slash up 1700 public sector jobs by 2032.

Although the government disputes the scale of the proposed staff reductions, when a new organisational chart was shown to staff in late September it identified “seven positions that were definitely to be cut,” Terry says. Those positions included two positions at the herbarium, a biologist, a graphic designer, a photographer, the museum’s only exhibitions officer, as well as the amalgamation of the vertebrate and invertebrate zoologist into a single role.

Asked about the government’s dismissal of the claims about a higher number of staff losing their jobs, Terry explains that over the last 12 months the museum has already lost “quite a lot of staff” through natural attrition and redundancies. “I suspect some of those positions were included in the 19.7 figure,” he says.

TMAG and the Tasmania state premier’s department has been approached for comment by The Art Newspaper.

According to independent budget analysis provided by the Friends of TMAG, the proposed changes under the broader cost-cutting initiative would also see TMAG move under the control of a new government agency called Building Tasmania and lose up to 27% of its funding for 2027-28 while its targets for physical visitation increase by 6.4%. TMAG is already “seriously underfunded”, says Terry. Its current exhibition Becoming Modern: Mid-century Australian Art has a 16-month run. “That's unheard of,” Terry continues, adding he thinks that “locals will be going less often because you're not going to go back many times to look at the same exhibition”.

A state government spokesperson says there is no correlation between the cost cutting measures and a new A$1.13bn (£573m) football stadium planned for Macquarie Point, a location that was once earmarked for a truth-and-reconciliation art park proposed by Dark Lab (a subsidiary of MONA). However, the independent MP Peter George asked in a statement issued on 25 September: “where’s the money [for that stadium] coming from?”

The proposed cuts to staff numbers are currently under review by the Tasmanian Industrial Commission and Tasmania’s Upper House is voting on calls to reverse cuts to TMAG’s budget. Decisions on both issues are expected on Tuesday 24 November.

At the time of writing both Gintaras Kantvilas, the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium and Simon Grove, a zoologist and curator of invertebrates, have said they have had their positions reinstated after they had been under threat due to the proposed cuts.

The development, which was due to address the genocide waged against Aboriginal Tasmanians by British colonists, has lost out to government-backed sports venue

#8912. Insta360’s X6 Winter Update Syncs 360° Video Capture with the Slopes App

Insta360’s X6 Winter Update Syncs 360° Video Capture with the Slopes App

Insta360 has announced a winter update for the X6 360-degree camera that ties footage to activity data in the popular ski and snowboard app Slopes, linking the footage to GPS data without needing a dedicated GPS accessory.

Slopes is a popular ski and snowboard app that provides digital trail maps for thousands of resorts worldwide. Because it is tied to a smartphone, the app tracks GPS data and provides riders with detailed information about their runs beyond just standard fitness data, such as top speed, average speed, lift versus run times, and more.

The Insta360 X6 now pairs with the Slopes app through the Insta360 app, providing riders with the ability to tie their footage to the data Slopes records. For example, “footage and data help riders review their progress and revisit moments from their season, from a favorite descent to a family ski day,” Insta360 explains.

“Riders can also connect their phone to X6 using the camera’s new Phone GPS Link feature. Once connected, X6 records GPS data with each shot, with no separate import step or dedicated GPS accessory required.”

Because the X6 captures 360-degree video, riders can combine that footage with the additional data provided by Slopes for specific cuts, like terrain or friends, as well as the ability to highlight specific runs.

“AI Director can identify highlights and assemble an edit,” Insta360 explains. “Dedicated skiing and snowboarding templates give riders another quick way to turn the day’s footage into a video they can share. When filming a friend, InstaFrame 2.0 keeps the selected skier or snowboarder in frame and produces a ready-to-share 4K flat video. With supported settings, 360 Video Backup also saves the full 360 degree view, so riders can go back and choose a different angle from the same run.”

The update to the Insta360 app, which allows the X6 to pair with the Slopes app, is free and will be available starting November 24. The integration will require a firmware update to the X6 as well, but that is performed through the app per usual. Slopes also requires a separate subscription.

#8910. TTArtisan’s AF 12mm f/2.8 Is a $489 Ultra-Wide Prime for Full-Frame Cameras

TTArtisan’s AF 12mm f/2.8 Is a $489 Ultra-Wide Prime for Full-Frame Cameras

TTArtisan has unveiled the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH., a new ultra-wide-angle lens for full-frame Sony and Nikon mirrorless cameras. Better still, it’s very affordable.

TTArtisan says its new lens is built for landscapes, architecture, and night-sky photography, all common applications for ultra-wide lenses. With its f/2.8 aperture, it should work well for astrophotography, though real-world performance will depend on how well it controls optical aberrations. For its part, TTArtisan promises “excellent aberration control” alongside “outstanding resolution,” even when shooting wide open.

The AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. lens has 16 optical elements arranged in 10 groups, including a pair of aspherical elements and three extra-low dispersion (ED) elements. The aperture diaphragm features just six blades, a relatively low count by modern standards, though it should produce distinct sunstars.

Many ultra-wide lenses are big, heavy, and difficult to use with traditional front filters, but the TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. is an exception. It weighs between 336 and 349 grams (11.85 to 12.31 ounces) and measures 72 to 74 millimeters (2.83 to 2.91 inches) long, with the Nikon Z-mount version being slightly heavier and longer than the Sony E-mount variant. The lens accepts common 82mm front filters, which is great news for landscape photographers who want to use circular polarizing and neutral-density filters. Because the front element is bulbous, mounting filters requires an extending filter-thread adapter, though TTArtisan includes one in the box and it adds minimal bulk.

The autofocus-equipped lens focuses as close as 0.18 meters (7.1 inches), making it well suited for emphasizing close-up foreground elements. Given its ultra-wide 122-degree field of view, though, it’s clearly not a macro lens. TTArtisan says the lens uses a high-performance stepping motor and supports eye- and face-detection autofocus modes on compatible cameras.

Speaking of compatibility, TTArtisan says the lens works seamlessly on Nikon Z-mount bodies, while some older Sony E-mount cameras have limited functionality. The Sony a7 III, for example, is fully compatible for photo modes but only partially compatible for video. The original a7 and a7 II also lack full compatibility. TTArtisan notes that autofocus performance may be limited on certain bodies, while firmware updates are in development for others. More compatibility details are available on the company’s website.

The TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. lens is available to preorder now for Nikon Z and Sony E-mount cameras at $489.

Although TTArtisan does not list an L-Mount version for sale, one is referenced on the product page. Since the company already makes several lenses for L-Mount, it is reasonable to expect the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. to arrive in that third mount down the road.

#8908. Nirvana Fans Raise $94K for Photographer Who Shot ‘Bleach’ Album Cover as She Battles Cancer

Nirvana Fans Raise $94K for Photographer Who Shot ‘Bleach’ Album Cover as She Battles Cancer

Nirvana fans have raised over $94,000 for the photographer who shot the cover of the band’s debut album Bleach, to cover her medical expenses as she enters hospice care.

Tracy Marander, the photographer behind the cover of Bleach and Kurt Cobain’s former girlfriend, has been battling cancer for four years. Last week, Marander’s family announced that the photographer was suspending her cancer treatment and entering hospice care.

Marander’s family launched a GoFundMe campaign to help cover her medical expenses, which has raised $94,101 toward its $100,000 goal at the time of writing. Hundreds of Nirvana fans have accompanied their donations with tributes to the photographer and her contribution to the band’s legacy.

Cobain’s widow Courtney Love also urged her followers to donate to the GoFundMe campaign in support of Marander in an Instagram post, calling the photographer “the unsung hero of Nirvana” who believed in the band’s lead singer “before he believed in himself.” In her post, Love describes the American medical system as “broken” and called on people to give what they could, adding “P.S. Kurt owed Tracy a lot of rent.”

A post shared by Courtney Love Cobain (@courtneylove)

Released in June 1989, Bleach was the debut studio album by Nirvana. Marander shot the iconic photograph that ended up becoming the album cover art during a Nirvana concert at Reko/Muse art gallery in Olympia, Washington, on April 1, 1989. Marander’s image shows the band performing live, with Cobain’s hair falling across his face, alongside guitarist Jason Everman, who did not play on the album despite appearing on its cover.

Lisa Orth, a graphic designer at the local music newspaper The Rocket, inverted the light and dark tones of Marander’s photograph to give it the appearance of a film negative. According to Nirvana: Taking Punk to the Masses by Jacob McMurray, Orth designed the album cover in keeping with the signature aesthetic of the band’s record label Sub Pop, which favored plain backgrounds, bold lettering, and striking photography. The cover also gave rise to Nirvana’s now-famous logo almost by accident, when Orth asked The Rocket’s typesetter Grant Alden to set the band’s name in whatever typeface was already installed on the typesetting machine.

Although Bleach received positive reviews from critics, it failed to enter the charts when it was first released. However, the album became popular when it was internationally reissued in 1992 following the commercial success of Nirvana’s second album Nevermind, released in 1991.

According to Nirvana biographer Michael Azerrad, Marander was Cobain’s first serious romantic partner and inspired him to write the song About a Girl. Their relationship lasted around three years before Cobain ended it in 1990. Marander recalled how Cobain encouraged her to develop her photographic talents, but the demands of working full-time and financially supporting him left her with little time to pursue her own creative interests.

“Near the end, we started fighting more and more,” Marander tells Azerrad in his 1993 book Come as You Are, according to reports. “He wanted me to be artistic, and I didn’t have time to be artistic. I was driving an hour to work and an hour back from work. I was supporting him.”

#8906. Cotswolds barn renovation by ConForm creates a "dialogue between old and new"

London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds, contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions.

Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.

ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a new contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.

“The design centres on a dialogue between old and new. Rather than blending the interventions into the existing fabric, we wanted each to remain legible and reinforce the other,” studio partner Ben Edgley told Dezeen.

“The building sits between two distinct parts of the farm: the older red brick buildings around the formal front farmyard and the more recent, industrial agricultural structures beyond,” he added.

“The design responds to both, retaining the brickwork and slate roof at the front while using zinc and blackened timber at the rear to reference the newer farm buildings.”

A defining feature of the barn’s new rear facade is a projecting volume wrapped by gabion walls, filled with locally-quarried stone and punctured by a large window illuminating a cross-laminated timber (CLT) staircase.

In the ground floor’s flexible office and arts spaces, the idea of material contrasts continues, with original red-brick walls and repaired timber ceilings accompanied by joinery including desks, storage and a bathroom pod in black through-coloured MDF.

Above, the guest apartment is tucked beneath the exposed beams of the barn’s roof, with its own dedicated living room, kitchen-diner and bathroom finished in matching black timber.

“The central CLT stair is the defining gesture. It brings together structure, circulation and spatial organisation, drawing the eye from the entrance through the building towards the trees beyond,” said Edgley.

“Its scale and material presence establish a clear contrast with the existing brickwork and timber frame,” he added.

“The clients were closely involved in the process, undertaking much of the timber repair alongside local craftsmen. Their commitment to retaining the original fabric was central to the project.”

ConForm Architects was founded in 2017 by Edgley alongside Eoin O’Leary.

Previous projects by the studio include a terraced home in London with perforated metal floors to filter daylight and a green-terrazzo flat extension modelled on bay windows.

#8904. Pelican Protector 2.0 vs YETI Gobox: Photo Gear Hardcase Throwdown!

Pelican Protector 2.0 vs YETI Gobox: Photo Gear Hardcase Throwdown!

With the release of the new Pelican Protector 2.0 Series and the YETI GoBox system with the KOR Insert, I decided to pit them against each other to see which gear case can take a beating and come out on top. And what better way to do it than to stuff them full of glass and roll them down a hill?

We get to conduct a rugged real-world test, and I get to let out my pent-up aggression—it’s a win-win! Both are new models, and the YETI is a brand-new product entirely, so let’s see how they hold up. Scroll to the bottom to see the full specs.

Pelican is the industry standard for transporting gear, and most of you have probably used one. This is the brand-new updated version of a case you already know, the 1510, now part of their Protector Series. There are a few improvements, though a lot of it looks very similar, if not the same, as the cases I already own.

The one solid improvement is the latches. They’re similar to what I have on my Pelican Air, and I’m glad they’re bringing this to the Protector Series at this size. Alongside the latch, there’s now a button that helps secure it. I’ve had this happen several times: I check a case onto a plane and it comes down the belt with a latch open, or worse, two latches open. The extra button keeps the latch from popping up on its own and requires an intentional force applied by a thumb to release the latch, which is a great addition.

Inside, the Pelican has a new lid organizer system compared to the classic Pelican foam. All the pouches are removable and you can shift them around, which is awesome. It also includes a light you can aim, dim, and change colors on, embedded right in the case, so you’re not fiddling with a headlamp every time you work in the dark.

You probably know YETI for coolers and backpacks, maybe not for cases. This is their contender to the Pelican 1510, and it’s similarly sized, so it’s clear they’re trying to get some skin in the gear cases game.

The design does indeed borrow a lot of familiar elements. There’s a top handle for rolling and wheels that are genuinely very smooth, with much less friction than the Pelican wheels. The latches are nice and big and require a two-part process, which is great for checked transport, and it has rubber seals for water resistance.

The one thing YETI offers that’s different is its packing system, which they call the KOR Insert. It comes with a pump, and the pump sucks the air out of these molds. You place your fragile items in between, close it up, and vacuum it down. The mold becomes rigid, forms around the object, and keeps it from wiggling. It’s ideal for transporting large, fragile items, though less useful for a bunch of small, different things like an assortment of camera accessories.

Aside from the packing system, the YETI looks durable but has more moving parts than the Pelican, which creates more potential for wear and tear, and eventually repair. The material is different too—the Pelican comes matte and feels like it can take a lot of scratches and bumps, while the YETI looks like it’ll scuff a bit more easily. Only one way to find out.

The starting weight of each case is worth flagging. The Pelican’s foam is super light, and everything comes in light. The YETI feels considerably heavier. If I’m packing heavy lenses, that starting weight becomes a problem for checking, since the limit on a lot of these is around 50 pounds or 22 kilograms.

The rolling handles differ too. The Pelican’s is all plastic, included at this size for a while now, and there’s no reason to change it. Minimal moving parts, one solid piece that can bend and take stress and hold up. The YETI uses what you’d see on a regular rolling suitcase: a button and aluminum rods that extend all the way up. Very smooth, but a lot more moving parts, and those are exactly the pieces that bend and break on suitcases. I can see having to replace that well before any plastic part on the Pelican.

To replicate how our luggage and airline agents treat delicate gear, I packed both with glass and went looking for a hill. For the record, the Pelican was loaded with six glass pieces while the YETI had four, and they feel about the same weight, which tells you plenty about the weight difference already.

First up, the Pelican down the hill. After the tumble, it still looked fresh and clean, no scratches I could see, and stickers still on. Inside, one of the flimsiest pieces survived, but the mason jar, which was supposed to be the tougher one, was busted. One out of six isn’t bad.

The YETI GoBox also fared well with the tumble, and all four pieces came out intact.

For a more real-world approach, I tossed both down a flight of stairs, as we are likely to see these things take more hard surface impacts. The Pelican held up well with all five of its remaining glasses surviving. The YETI came through mostly fine, but one piece was busted this time — the fragile stemmed glass. The KOR Insert maintained its shape.

As a bonus, I wanted to see how each handled a single heavy impact at one point, so I took a sledgehammer to them, which was perhaps the most surprising test result. Both cases bounced the hammer back like a trampoline, with no dent or scratch at the point of impact. They passed the smash test with flying colors.

Both cases size up well, and you can fit a lot in either. Pelican is the clear winner for small lenses, accessories, and the bags and pouches, though it can still take a large gear item with the right laser-cut or custom foam insert.

The YETI with KOR Insert is less suited for small items, but the insert does allow for large items with intricate or unusual forms, and can be reused and reshaped for any items that can fit inside of it. Pelican slightly outperforms YETI in terms of ruggedness and repair simplicity, but both stood up to our beatings pretty well. Hopefully, this gives you enough info to choose the right case for you.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#8900. Efforts to save I.M. Pei’s Dallas City Hall likely headed to referendum

The campus of the modernist Dallas City Hall, built in 1978 and designed by I.M. Pei, includes Marta Pan’s Floating Sculpture (1973, foreground) Photo: D Guest Smith, via Alamy Stock Photo

When the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M. Pei’s city hall in 1978, he called it “a monument to the city’s pride, a symbol of a first-class city that’s reaching for greatness”. The seven-storey inverted pyramid slopes over a large plaza with site-specific sculptures like Henry Moore’s Vertebra in Three Pieces (1978, also known as The Dallas Piece) and Marta Pan’s Floating Sculpture (1973), which sits in a reflecting pool.

Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers. They have cited the prohibitive costs of renovating the building, which ballooned within a matter of months from $81m according to an initial estimate for a basic infrastructure upgrade to $1.4bn for massive upgrades over two decades.

In recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor. He has called the building “obsolete”. Architecturally significant or not, moving the municipal headquarters “would make this location available for development, which I would also support. I believe that will be a very, very big part of the future of downtown and its revitalisation.” Spokespersons for the city did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s questions.

The current mayor is in alignment with the “Say Yes to Downtown” campaign group led by former mayor Mike Rawlings. With developers and other former leaders, the campaign argues that city hall must be demolished to create an entertainment district, including a new arena for two of the city’s professional sports teams, the Dallas Mavericks basketball team and the Stars hockey team. When the teams announced plans to move out of the city’s core, both considered relocating to the city hall site. They ultimately chose other locations.

Amid the uproar over the possible demolition of Pei’s modernist complex, few have questioned the fate of Pan’s and Moore’s sculptures. Both were gifted to the city and are part of the municipal public art collection. But the future of Moore’s, which has required previous renovation, in part with help from the artist’s London-based estate and foundation, is a particular concern. The large grouping of organic forms was meant to complement Pei’s rigidly angular structure. It was also a gift to the city from the philanthropist W.R. Hawn in memory of his wife Mildred Hawn, whose favourite sculptor was Moore. Both sculptures are part of the preservation plan for the building; representatives for Moore and Pan’s estates did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries.

Dallas City Hall The Lyda Hill Texas Collection of Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

The non-profit Save Dallas City Hall, an ideologically diverse grassroots coalition, has been among the loudest voices opposed to moving the facility. It is led by president Bruce Richardson, a musician, artist and former political candidate, and vice-president Zaida Basora, an architect and former city employee who oversaw maintenance of properties, including city hall, and currently serves as the executive director of the American Institute of Architects Dallas.

Basora and her colleagues have proposed a ten-year phased plan that, even factoring in inflation, is estimated to cost between $70m and $100m, and would not require municipal staff to move. The cost of simply demolishing the building—to say nothing of the expense of building something in its place—has been estimated at $60m.

The Dallas city council gave Tolbert a deadline of 26 August to present relocation options for city hall, which she missed. Inflation has also increased the cost of relocating. The same month, Save Dallas City Hall sued the city, arguing that it was committing “demolition by neglect”.

“Dallas city hall has at least one failed generator, active parking garage leaks and is due for roof maintenance,” Richardson said in a statement. “Instead of tackling these problems with millions in available funds, the city halted repairs, wasting money and time to explore a move.”

On 2 October, the Save Dallas City Hall coalition started an effort to gather signatures to create a ballot referendum on the fate of city hall, which would be put to residents for a vote in May 2027. In early November, the group announced it had gathered around 25,000 signatures—well over the minimum 20,000 signatures needed for a ballot referendum. If the group’s proposed amendment to the city charter passes next spring, the municipal government will be required to continue operating from Pei’s city hall.

During elections earlier this month, 56% of Dallas voters opposed a $443m bond package. That package had included funding to move emergency operations out of city hall, which, according to advocates of preserving Pei’s building, would have been a first step toward abandoning it.

For the local activist Stephanie Drenka, a co-founder of the Dallas Asian American Historical Society who has spoken at nearly every public hearing since she learned of the building’s significance, preserving city hall is essential to recognising Pei’s contribution to Asian American history.

“The stakes are beyond our city alone,” she says. Less than 1% of historic markers in the US acknowledge the contributions of Asian Americans, according to the national non-profit Asian & Pacific Islander Americans in Historic Preservation.

“This also makes demolition of city hall an issue of further erasure of Asian Americans in history,” Drenka says. “It’s not just Pei’s legacy, but we’re defending ourselves. Everything in our community is embodied in this building.” She adds: “If we can’t save city hall then what threat can we stop?”

#8899. Jimmy Chin’s Jaw-Dropping Photo Shot on iPhone Makes TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026

Jimmy Chin’s Jaw-Dropping Photo Shot on iPhone Makes TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026

TIME has released its annual Top 100 Photos of the Year feature, celebrating striking images that capture the biggest moments and events of 2026. One of the featured photos was shot by acclaimed photographer and filmmaker Jimmy Chin using the iPhone 18 Pro, marking a milestone for Apple’s latest flagship smartphone and, of course, Chin himself.

Chin, an Academy Award-winning director, National Geographic photographer, and accomplished mountaineer, photographed his longtime climbing partner, Conrad Anker, as part of a new series, What Holds Us. Chin and Anker have climbed together for 25 years, scaling peaks around the world.

“What I was after was that intersection: human ambition in pursuit of awe and wonder, set against a landscape that was here long before us and will be here long after,” Chin explains.

“Out there you are reminded how small you are. That has always put things in perspective for me, and I hope it does for whoever is standing in front of the picture.”

For Chin, who has shot in many extreme and remote locations throughout his career, the smaller and lighter the gear, the better.

“A production puts something between you and the person in front of you — gear, crew, the apparatus of a shoot. Working this way there was no apparatus. It was just the two of us, which is the only condition under which that kind of ease shows up in a frame,” Chin continues.

Using Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro, Chin was able to travel lighter without sacrificing performance or image quality. As his photo above shows, the iPhone 18 Pro more than delivered — a testament to just how far smartphone imaging technology has come. Chin is far from the only photographer or filmmaker to integrate an iPhone into a professional workflow in recent years.

Chin shot 48MP ProRAW photos the iPhone 18 Pro and then stitched multiple shots to create one of his signature panoramas. The final photo is over 300 megapixels and 25,000 pixels wide. There’s no question it holds up extremely well in the large print featured in the What Holds Us exhibit.

Chin’s photos are also part of the What Holds Us exhibition, curated by Kathy Ryan, appearing alongside works by Alex Prager and Jack Davison. After debuting in New York City in September, the exhibition opens in London on December 4, running at Saatchi Yates Gallery through December 13.

Image creditsJimmy Chin unless otherwise noted.

#8897. CLB Architects creates ADU in Wyoming with rock-climbing wall

US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple.

The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of Jackson. The site is dotted with mature trees and sits along the west bank of the Snake River.

Before the project’s inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.

As their son neared graduation from high school, the couple decided to build an ADU on the property and make it their full-time residence, while renting out the main residence.

“The new house would allow them to remain on the land they had known for decades, while experiencing it in a new way – closer to nature, with stronger connections to light, views and outdoor living,” said Jackson-based CLB Architects.

The house also represents a way to accommodate a growing need for housing while preserving the natural landscape.

“In our region, there’s a clear need for this housing type, which is economical, compact and responsive to place,” said CLB Architects partner Eric Logan.

A primary challenge for the design team was to ensure the house “met the couple’s programmatic and budget constraints” within a very compact footprint. Per country regulations, the new house could not exceed 1,000 square feet (92.9 square metres).

The architects conceived a simple, rectangular volume that rises two levels and is topped with a gabled roof. The house was carefully sited so it would feel separate from the main residence.

“Siting the building toward the back of the parcel and introducing new landscaping and tree plantings created a soft buffer between the two dwellings,” the architect said.

The team carved out portions of the exterior to form inset terraces, along with a climbing wall that is used by the couple’s son while home from college. On the east-facing elevation, a boxy protrusion forms a balcony.

Both inside and out, the team opted for materials that were durable, cost-efficient and complemented the building’s form. Dark corrugated metal clads most of the building, while tight-knot cedar was used for inset areas to provide “warmth and depth”.

The ground level contains a spacious garage for vehicles and outdoor gear. The upper level holds two bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms, all of which are organised around a central living area.

“Locating the main living spaces on the second floor allows the interiors to engage the tree canopy while maximising natural light, offering a more intimate relationship with the landscape,” the team said.

The living area opens onto a west-facing deck, which acts as an “outdoor living room” for much of the year. Large, sliding glass doors diminish the boundary between inside and out and usher in breezes during summer months.

The clients, both of whom have deep experience in design and construction fields, poured themselves into the project. The husband served as the general contractor and engaged local tradespeople to help out.

“A true labor of love, the couple built much of the house themselves, working on the construction every evening and on weekends,” the team said, noting the project was completed in about nine months.

The project offers ideas for how communities in the Mountain West can accommodate growth while preserving the natural landscape.

“With rising land values and the need to accommodate more residents, homes like this – that are compact, efficient, and contextual – can provide more housing while preserving open space,” the team said.

“As local communities grapple with growth, projects like this suggest one path forward.”

Other ADUs in America include a small, cedar-clad dwelling in California’s wine country by Schwartz and Architecture, and a compact, metal-clad building in Austin by North Arrow Studio that resembles a birdhouse.

#8895. US affordable artists' housing initiatives hobbled by uneven regulation and oversight

Artist Emilie Dundee Odeile has exhibited at a state-subsidised arts project in Trinidad, Colorado Courtesy Dundee & Lee

“Affordability” is on the lips of every American. In Colorado, over 35% of residents spend more than 30% of their income on housing, which is considered a cost burden by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (Hud). The state is responding by allocating $300m annually to the State Affordable Housing Fund. A niche area of this investment is the development of affordable housing for artists and creative districts.

National non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort. Both non-profits market affordable housing for artists, but in the absence of artist certification programmes such as those in Boston, New York and now San Francisco, restricting available affordable housing to artists could run the risk of violating fair housing laws. There are also few mechanisms for cities and states to ensure their public funding delivers long-term solutions for artists’ housing and creative spaces.

“We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border. The artists used around 152 miles of yarn to bring the famous children’s book to life in a 2023 exhibition.

“We started our RV-life, one-year road trip experiment,” Chapin says. “We were on our way to Santa Fe, and went through Trinidad”—and they never left. Goodnight Moon and another project by Odeile debuted at Space to Create, a state-led initiative to produce creative workforce housing and studios in rural Colorado.

Trinidad was the first municipality identified by the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade (OEDIT) for public investment through the establishment of a creative district, in 2015. Today, 37 creative districts exist across the state. Next door to Space to Create on Trinidad’s historic Main Street, Artspace manages residences for artists.

Artspace develops and operates workforce housing across 23 states, including seven projects in Colorado. Each project markets itself “for those in the creative sector” and offers residential space that “prioritises creative use”. But without a formal certification programme to identify artists in Colorado or any of the local municipalities it operates in, it is unclear how Artspace can legally give preference to artist applicants over members of the general public.

Poet and editor Michele McDannold lived in Artspace’s complex in Michigan City, Indiana, for nearly four years and at the organisation’s Honolulu location for seven months. She arrived in Trinidad in 2020, but noticed a substantial difference in the artist preference process at that location compared to the properties she had been in previously. In Michigan City, she says, “I had to give a presentation to a board of practicing artists and participate in an interview.” In Trinidad, she was only asked to submit information for income eligibility. McDannold has only encountered five artists across the property’s 40 units during her three-year stay. The result of not prioritising artist applicants appeared to be that there were almost no artist residents.

“When it came time to organise or participate in something like [open studios or a gallery night],” McDannold says, “neighbours were like, ‘What? Why are you bothering me?”

Artspace did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s multiple requests for comment. The Artspace Trinidad leasing office stated that it does not track the number of artist residents at that location.

Affordable housing is a broad term that lives on a spectrum of interpretation and regulation. According to the federal government, household affordability is based on the regional or area median income (AMI). What a property owner can charge a tenant is determined by Hud’s AMI calculations, but a lender can set the contractual terms of the tax credit, loan or grant, whether private or public. Under US Treasury regulations, a housing unit generates a low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) only if it is available for general-public use. However, in 2008 the Housing and Economic Recovery Act added a provision to the Internal Revenue Service’s tax code stating that general-public use is not violated if preference is given to tenants involved in artistic or literary activities. Even so, some cities maintain their own artist certification programmes for affordable housing.

A 2023 affordable housing audit by Denver’s Department of Housing Stability expressed concerns that priority access to housing could violate the federal Fair Housing Act. While the report specifically focused on the Denver city council’s move to prioritise displaced households or people at risk of displacement, it highlighted the fact that prioritising seniors and veterans also requires better systems for monitoring and evaluation. Each time a person, such as an artist, is prioritised for affordable housing access, the county must track data such as the number of units allocated, eligibility requirements, types of document accepted as evidence of eligibility, the selection process, and the parties responsible for implementation and monitoring the property and rent levels.

Municipal governments are concerned about incurring fair housing lawsuits, especially if state and county laws contradict or fail to reaffirm the 2008 tax code revision. Cities considering allocating affordable housing units for artists can be faced with having to develop significant compliance procedures. This patchwork of rules, requirements and compliance regimes helps explain why creating and maintaining affordable housing for artists can be very complicated, costly, and look different in different cities and regions. According to the Center for an Urban Future, US cities have created just 2,804 units of dedicated housing for artists in the last decade.

The soaring windows of 210 East Street in Trinidad must have caught the eye of the developer Dana Crawford when she first visited the elegant century-old school building. Crawford, who died in January 2025, was a celebrated preservationist in the region, known for saving Denver’s historic Larimer Square and redeveloping the city’s Union Station. There were minimal requirements attached to the $4m community revitalisation grant Crawford received for the redevelopment of 210 East Street into 17 affordable live-work spaces for artists. An open records request reveals the terms of the grant for the property only ask for progress reports on the number of housing units and jobs created.

The Former East Street School building in Trinidad, Colorado has been converted to housing and marketed as affordable for artists, among others Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust

For the 210 East Street project, Crawford procured three different tax credits, the $4m community revitalisation grant and $1.8m in private financing, but the most restrictive terms were attached to last-minute funding from the city of Trinidad. In 2022 Crawford applied to the city’s Housing Now incentive programme to help cover the $125,000 cost of redesigning five units. The city approved the request on the condition of a two-year workforce housing deed restriction, requiring rent rates to be limited to 80% of AMI starting in 2023.

Crawford also sought $1.9m in funding from an impact investor, Greenland CDF. The funding from Greenland was contingent on signing a Community Benefit Agreement (CBA), a binding contract that requires the borrower to produce a social benefit with enforceable penalties. The details of the agreement are not public and expired earlier this year.

Less than five years after Crawford received a total of $7.5m in public funding for 210 East Street, the property was acquired by Cast. There are no existing public terms that legally require Cast to deliver affordable housing to artists, or even general housing.

Cast operates a non-profit real estate development strategy around creative spaces and affordability. Recently, the organisation expanded that strategy to housing in Colorado.

“Our model as a non-profit is to reset the floor of affordability,” says Ken Ikeda, Cast’s chief executive. “If we could do that without debt, through grants, then that would keep it that way in perpetuity.”

Currently, Ikeda adds, Cast is only required to deliver the private terms of the $1.9m grant the organisation received from the Colorado Health Foundation to acquire 210 East Street. Rent at the complex is currently between 55% and 80% of AMI, and according to a spokesperson for the organisation, five current residents are artists. The Art Newspaper was only able to verify that one resident is an artist, and that person said they know of no others.

Half a mile from 210 East Street are three properties that have received significant public funding in exchange for affordable artists’ housing. In 2019 ownership of two addresses on Main Street and one on Elm Street were transferred to Artspace by the city of Trinidad. In exchange for that real estate and a $715,000 promissory note by the Colorado Housing Finance Authority in 2022, Artspace must deliver housing units within or below 40% to 60% of AMI for 35 years, and preserve the historic facade of the Main Street properties for 15 years. If it fails to maintain this commitment, it must repay the borrowed funds.

The vastly different requirements for the Artspace and Cast properties in Trinidad, and the strings attached (or not) to their public and private funding reflect the wildly different standards and requirements for organisations creating and operating affordable artists’ housing.

The 444 17th Street building in Denver, the future site of a multi-use affordable housing and cultural hub for artists, to be operated by Community Arts Stabilization Trust Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust

A vibrant art and culture scene boosts local businesses and helps create jobs, according to the Denver Downtown Development Authority (DDDA), a city initiative to revive a downtown core where the vacancy rate has remained at or above 30% since the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2025 and 2026 the DDDA awarded $114.5m in financing for new housing and $4.45m for art-related initiatives—including a $1.35m grant to Cast to convert 6,300 sq. ft of vacant office and retail space into affordable artists’ studios, a cinema and gallery. The city council approved the terms of the property’s sale to Cast in September.

“We are going to make it affordable no matter what, because that is our aim and objective,” Ikeda says of the project in Denver, which has been vacant since 2021. Cast estimates the art space will open in the summer of 2027.

Representatives for the city did not clarify how it defines “affordable” in the context of commercial real estate, but noted that the city has the first right to purchase the property for $1 for the next ten years if Cast decides to sell. In the meantime, municipal support will be released in phases as Cast reaches a series of build-out milestones.

While Denver finds its footing on affordable housing for artists and New York has not added any units in a decade, San Francisco’s first dedicated affordable artists’ housing is on track to open in 2028. The Artist Hub on Market, at 1687 Market Street, will have 94 units of housing, rehearsal space and a theatre. Rent will be set between 30% and 80% of the AMI, depending on the size of the unit and number of occupants, which equates to annual income of between $46,440 and $167,120 for tenants.

A rendering of the future Artists Hub on Market project in San Francisco Courtesy Artists Hub on Market and Mercy Housing California

Launching alongside the Market Street property is a new artist certification programme for San Francisco, facilitated by the Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development. Artists can achieve certification by documenting at least $10,000 in annual income from their art practice, showing proof of a public art commission or grant in the previous three years, or submitting a portfolio of work for review. Once certification is awarded, artists can enter the lottery for units at Artist Hub on Market; any units unclaimed by artists in the lottery will be opened to general-public use through the city’s affordable housing system.

Of the Artist Hub on Market project’s $140m in funding, $100m came from a single anonymous donor and, according to a source familiar with the terms of the deal, implementing the artist certification programme was a condition of the funding.

The inconsistent regulation of properties that receive public funding for affordable artists’ housing and cultural spaces risks undermining such projects’ longevity and disappointing the communities they were meant to serve. Recently, a $400,000 low-interest loan from the DDDA to Denver Immersive Repertory Theater (Dirt) went into default after Dirt’s alleged failure to make rent payments less than a year after it was awarded the loan and before its project ever opened to the public. According to reporting by Denverite, the loan’s rate surges from 3% to 15% when loan proceeds are shown to not be used for their intended purpose, though it is unclear what assets the city will be able to claw back from the project’s founders.

Affordable housing for artists is an emerging sector entangled with various local governments’ goals, which include attracting business, lowering housing costs by adding units and retaining creative workers. Ikeda describes every affordability project as a funding “butterfly” due to the unique risks and complexity of the capital and terms assembled. But, he adds, they are worth the trouble: “There is something magical about artist-only housing and live-work environments.”

While it is not a central topic in their campaigns, Andrew Cuomo, Zohran Mamdani and Curtis Sliwa have all addressed issues relevant to artists and arts workers

#8894. 13 Winners From the The Royal Photographic Society Awards 2026

13 Winners From the The Royal Photographic Society Awards 2026

The Royal Photographic Society (RPS) has announced the recipients of its 2026 Awards, with cinematographer Sir Roger Deakins among this year’s honorees.

Deakins has received the RPS Centenary Medal, the Society’s most prestigious honor. Widely regarded as one of the greatest cinematographers in film history, Deakins has won two Academy Awards for Best Cinematography and five BAFTA Awards in the same category.

British photographer Timon Benson has received the RPS Award for Achievement in the Art of Photography (under 30). At the beginning of his career, Benson was already attracting significant national and international recognition. His work spans documentary photography, choreography, and abstraction, exploring the nature of photography and its relationship with contemporary life.

The RPS Progress Medal in the Science of Photography has been awarded to Professor Marc Levoy, an American computer graphics researcher and Professor Emeritus of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. Levoy is also a vice president and fellow at Adobe and a Distinguished Engineer at Google.

British photographic artist Mandy Barker is the recipient of The RPS Award for Environmental Responsibility. Barker is internationally recognized for her work documenting marine plastic debris. Working alongside scientists, she uses photography to highlight the scale of plastic pollution in the world’s oceans and its impact on marine life and the wider environment.

Documentary photographer and filmmaker Polly Braden has received the RPS Award for Social Impact. Her long-term collaborative projects explore how people live and work, and their place in society. Her latest project, Against the Tide, produced with The Guardian, followed young people in 17 coastal towns. The project was exhibited at Arnolfini in Bristol and Firstsite in Colchester, and also brought 16 young people to Parliament to give evidence to MPs.

Now in its 148th year, the Royal Photographic Society Awards date back to 1878. The Society describes them as the world’s longest-running photography awards. They recognize achievements across still and moving images, celebrating individuals rather than individual photographs. The awards cover a broad range of disciplines, including moving image, new media, science and imaging, education, publishing, and curation.

Victoria Humphries, CEO of the Royal Photographic Society, says the awards reflect the breadth of the photographic community and the many ways people contribute to the medium.

“The RPS Awards provide an opportunity to recognize and celebrate those who are making a difference, whether through their creativity, innovation, research, education or their contribution to the wider photographic community,” Humphries says.

“As an organization, we believe that photography is for everyone, and these RPS Awards demonstrate that there are so many different ways to engage with, contribute to and shape its future.”

Deakins says he is particularly pleased to be recognized for his still photography, given his career in cinematography.

“I’m very honored to receive this award from the Royal Photographic Society. Although I have been more known for my work in cinematography, still photography has always been a passion and more personal to me. To be recognized by the Royal Photographic Society for my work in stills is amazing and means a great deal to me.”

The complete list of RPS 2026 Awards Recipients is available here.

#8891. Rare 1889 Photo of Historic New York Giants Baseball Team Is Up for Auction

Rare 1889 Photo of Historic New York Giants Baseball Team Is Up for Auction

A rare cabinet photograph of the New York Giants, one of early professional baseball’s most significant teams, taken by renowned baseball photographer Joseph Hall in 1889, is up for auction.

One of Major League Baseball’s oldest franchises, the New York Giants rose to prominence in the late 19th century, winning back-to-back championships in 1888 and 1889, before the modern World Series was established in 1903. The team boasted several future Baseball Hall of Famers during this era. Its legacy continues today as the San Francisco Giants, following the franchise’s relocation from New York to California in 1958.

The photograph, which is being offered by auction house Huggins & Scott as part of a sale which runs through December 3, features the New York Giants team that won the 1888 World Championship. The auction house says it has never handled another example of this particular photograph in its imperial cabinet format, making it one of the rarest of Joseph Hall’s baseball team photographs.

Hall photographed many of the Major League baseball teams in 1888 and was widely regarded as the leading baseball photographer of the late 1880s. Hall’s cabinet photographs of professional baseball teams and players are among the most sought-after photographic collectibles of the late 19th century, with his images of teams posing in uniform at ballparks commanding the highest prices.

While a smaller cabinet card featuring the same image of the Giants appeared at auction several years ago, Huggins & Scott says it cannot recall seeing another example of this photograph in this larger format. According to the auction house, the size and quality of the print are particularly noteworthy given the limitations of photographic production in the late 19th century. Producing photographs of this scale and quality required a considerable investment of time and resources, and the auction house suggests that only a small number of prints may have been made.

Unlike other photographs Hall took of the Giants that feature an outdoor stadium background, the image shows 19 members of the team posing together in a studio. Among those pictured are six future Baseball Hall of Famers: Tim Keefe, Roger Connor, Buck Ewing, Jim O’Rourke, John Montgomery Ward, and Mickey Welch.

The photograph is up for sale in the Fall Auction at Huggins & Scott Auctions, which runs through December 3.

#8889. New York Times Prohibits Photographers From Using Photoshop 2027

New York Times Prohibits Photographers From Using Photoshop 2027

The latest version of Adobe Photoshop, Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0), added many AI-powered photo-editing features. Not all photographers are thrilled about the increasingly heavy focus on generative AI inside Photoshop, and photojournalists are taking note, too.

As The Verge reports, The New York Times sent an email to freelance photographers and contributors warning them against using Adobe Photoshop 2027.

The email, which was shared on social media, specifically cites features inside Photoshop that use generative AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.”

The Times‘ worries about Photoshop 28.0.0 are more about a perceived lack of clarity surrounding the application’s photo-editing features than the presence of AI itself. Photoshop has included generative AI in many tools for years, including Generative Remove and Generative Expand. The latest release uses generative AI for even more tasks, such as relighting and restyling photos.

New York Times photojournalists and freelance contributors cannot use generative AI on their photos. In fact, as the publication’s ethics standards outline, all published photos must be accurate depictions of real events. This means no people or objects can be added, rearranged, blurred, distorted, or removed. It also means that cropping must be done carefully so as not to omit any relevant details in a scene. Color can be adjusted, but only minimally and in service of accurately reproducing an event as it happened.

The Times adds that any use of AI, including generative AI, must be clearly disclosed to readers. The organization has long embraced Adobe’s C2PA initiative as it relates to image provenance and metadata, and that is not changing.

What has changed, apparently, is how easy it is for a photographer to inadvertently use a feature inside Adobe Photoshop that relies on generative AI, which will then show up in the metadata. This appears to be the primary concern for The New York Times, as it cannot work with photos that are labeled as AI-edited content.

“It has come to our attention that certain functions in Adobe Photoshop 2027 utilize generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to users of the software. At this time we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using this new version when working on assignment for The Times,” New York Times spokesperson Graham James tells PetaPixel.

To prevent these issues, all contributing photographers must entirely avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignments for The Times—an unprecedented blow to Photoshop’s already wavering reputation among professional photographers. Fortunately, it is possible for users to install previous versions of Photoshop through the Creative Cloud app, although it’s not necessarily straightforward. As of this writing, users can roll back to Photoshop 27.0, but no earlier.

Adobe’s insistence on publicizing its generative AI features, rather than the genuinely good and mostly inoffensive improvements made earlier this month to Adobe Camera Raw and Lightroom, has created quite a stir in the photography community. The Times‘s new policy will certainly not help Adobe’s PR problem with photographers.

PetaPixel reached out to Adobe for comment but did not hear back ahead of publication. This story will be updated with any response.

#8887. NASA Spacecraft Snaps Moody Photo of Earth on Its Way to Mars

NASA Spacecraft Snaps Moody Photo of Earth on Its Way to Mars

NASA’s ESCAPADE spacecraft has captured an incredible photo of the Earth as it slingshotted past the planet on its way to Mars.

The images were taken by the spacecraft’s Visible and Infrared Observation System camera, developed by Northern Arizona University, at around 9 A.M. EST on November 9. This was approximately three hours after the spacecraft made its closest approach to Earth, when it was about 38,500 miles away and had a clear view of the Western Hemisphere.

The images were captured by the second of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft to perform a powered flyby of Earth this month. Both spacecraft used a combination of engine burns and Earth’s gravity to gain momentum for their 10-month journey to Mars.

Once they reach orbit around the Red Planet, the spacecraft will study how the solar wind — a stream of charged particles traveling at around a million miles per hour from the Sun — interacts with Mars’ environment and contributes to the loss of its atmosphere.

A commercial satellite captured images of the pair from approximately 3,000 miles away, while a member of the mission team photographed the spacecraft passing overhead from his home near Los Angeles (below).

Two spacecraft. Two flybys. One path to Mars.

Photographed from the Los Angeles area, Blue and Gold streaked through the same part of the sky two days apart—Blue in blue, Gold in gold. https://t.co/9SDOMmqqtY

— Rocket Lab (@RocketLab) November 23, 2026

NASA explains that the ESCAPADE mission is funded by NASA’s Heliophysics Division and is part of the agency’s Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration program. The University of California, Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory leads the mission, working with partners including Rocket Lab, NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Advanced Space, and Blue Origin.
