Let's make this concrete. You've been paying $1,800/month in rent for the past year, diligently hitting your five monthly transactions. Your Bilt account holds approximately 21,600 points (1x on rent, plus some bonus earning on the card). You're planning a long weekend in Nashville with your partner.

The Property: Hyatt Place Nashville Downtown. Category 3, costing 12,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Cash rate for a Friday–Sunday stay: $189/night, totaling $378 for two nights before taxes and fees. With taxes, you're looking at roughly $430 out of pocket.

The Points Play: Transfer 24,000 Bilt points to Hyatt instantly, book two nights. Total points spent: 24,000. Total cash paid: $0 (Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges, no award fees).

The CPP calculation: $378 cash value ÷ 24,000 points = 1.58 cents per point at the conservative end. Factor in the taxes you're also avoiding (most properties don't charge taxes on award stays), and your effective CPP climbs closer to 1.8–2 cents per point.

Now scale up. Apply the same 24,000 points to a single night at Park Hyatt Chicago — a Category 7 property. Cash rate: $550–$700/night on a peak weekend. Points cost: 30,000 per night (you'll need to save a couple extra months). At $600 cash value for 30,000 points, you're at 2 cents per point — but if you hit a $700 night, that's 2.33 cpp.

The experience itself? Park Hyatt properties deliver: floor-to-ceiling windows, complimentary minibar items, a spa, and a level of service that genuinely doesn't feel like a "points hotel." You're not using a coupon at a budget chain — you're staying at the same property business travelers expense at full rate, experiencing everything they experience, funded almost entirely by the rent check you wrote anyway.

If you hold Hyatt Globalist status, suite upgrades on award stays are available based on availability — turning a 30,000-point redemption into a $900+ suite night. That's where the CPP ceiling of 8 cents per point becomes real.

World of Hyatt awards include a fifth-night-free benefit on standard award redemptions when you book five or more consecutive nights. On a five-night stay at a Category 5 property (20,000 points/night), you'd normally pay 100,000 points — but with the fifth night free, it's 80,000 points for five nights. That's a 20% improvement in value with zero extra effort. Plan longer trips to unlock this.

Do: Book 395 Days Out for Peak Destinations

Hyatt opens award inventory at the same time as cash inventory — 395 days in advance. For high-demand properties (think Park Hyatt Maldives at Hadahaa or Alila Ventana Big Sur), availability at standard rates disappears quickly. Set a calendar reminder and search early.

If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, your Chase Ultimate Rewards points also transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. This means you have two separate point pools feeding the same program — Bilt for rent earnings and Chase for everyday spending. Together, you can accumulate Hyatt points significantly faster and take on higher-category properties.

Avoid: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

Bilt-to-Hyatt transfers are instant and irreversible. If you transfer 30,000 points and then can't find the availability you thought you saw, those points are now in Hyatt — and if you don't use them, they expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Always search Hyatt first, confirm dates and property, then transfer.

Avoid: Missing the 5-Transaction Monthly Minimum

This is the most common Bilt mistake. If you forget to make five purchases on your Bilt card in a given month, you earn zero points on rent — not reduced points, zero. Automate five small recurring charges to the card and never think about it again.

Do: Target Category 4–6 Properties for Best Value

Category 1–3 properties offer solid value, but the CPP accelerates meaningfully in Categories 4–6 (15,000–25,000 points/night) where cash rates are $200–$400 but points costs haven't kept pace. This is the sweet spot within the sweet spot.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards

Hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

This redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

This isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. The ChooseFI community has embraced this one for good reason — it's genuinely the most accessible entry point into premium hotel travel rewards available today.

No. Bilt works with any landlord that accepts payment. If your building is not in the Bilt Alliance, Bilt processes the payment via ACH. The only difference is Alliance buildings may offer additional perks like bonus points or rent credits.

You will still pay your rent through Bilt, but you will earn zero points on that month's rent payment. The five-transaction requirement resets monthly. Set up autopay on small recurring charges to prevent this.

Yes. Bilt transfers to over a dozen airline and hotel partners including American Airlines, United, Air Canada Aeroplan, and IHG. However, Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value among hotel transfer partners.

Bilt caps rent earning at 100,000 points per month (equivalent to $100,000 in rent at 1x). For the vast majority of renters, this cap is irrelevant. There is no annual cap on total points earned.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Bilt-to-Hyatt pipeline is the most accessible travel rewards sweet spot available today. You are already paying rent. The Bilt card has no annual fee. Hyatt points deliver 2-8 cents in value. The transfer is instant. If you rent and you are not earning Hyatt points from that rent payment, you are leaving hundreds of dollars in annual hotel value on the table. Start with one Category 3-4 weekend stay to see it work, then scale up to aspirational properties as your balance grows.

#8845. A New Museum in Georgia’s Wine Country Shows Another Side of the Country’s Art History

A long journey from Tokyo to the island of Naoshima to see art gave Jemal Inaishvili, a shipping executive and collector, an idea for how he might convince people to make a similar trek within his home country of Georgia in the South Caucasus. Unlike visiting Naoshima, which typically involves a full day of travel, the drive from the capital city of Tbilisi to Kakheti, Georgia’s eastern wine region, is around two hours, three in heavy traffic. “Of course, I cannot copy them,” he told me recently, “but I will do something similar, but based on Georgian art.”

The result is the Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, which opened to the public earlier this month on land Inaishvili bought a decade ago for a small winery. The site now also holds a hotel, a sculpture park, and a red-slatted museum with a rooftop for performances and film screenings by the Tbilisi practice Midamo. This admission-free venue will stage four exhibitions a year, drawing from Inaishvili’s collection of about 1,000 works.

To lead the programming, Inaishvili has hired 28-year-old Nino Sulkhanishvili. “Sometimes one’s experience will be the barrier,” he said of the creative director, who is in her first institutional role. “Together with the foundation, she is also growing.”

In heading up a private museum, Sulkhanishvili sees her role as helping to give Georgian artists the infrastructure to exhibit at home, like Elene Chantladze, whose solo show will open at the Kvareli Foundation in February. Such a setting, Sulkhanishvili said, “is extremely important, especially in your own country. … I feel Georgian artists deserve much more.” Location, too, matters: “contemporary art needs to be decentralized,” she said, noting the foundation’s aim to create an art ecosystem by bringing schoolchildren to visit and training local guides. A residency for both local and international artists will launch next year.

But Georgian art won’t be the foundation’s only focus after the first two years. The collection also includes work by Ukrainian, Turkish, and Armenian artists, which will be shown in the future. In the years to come, Sulkhanishvili hopes to build exchanges with neighboring and post-Soviet countries before looking further afield. “We really want to be a beacon within the region,” she said.

The inaugural exhibition, “Georgian Contemporary Art: Origins and Continuities” (on view through January 15), came together only six months before opening. Instead of just focusing solely on Inaishvili’s collection, Sulkhanishvili proposed a historical survey of the artists who worked outside the Soviet era’s state-sanctioned socialist realism. The show gathers 57 artists from the 1960s to the present, with roughly half the works from his collection and the rest on loan. “Even in the national museums, you don’t see everything together,” Sulkhanishvili said of the artists on view, many of whom are still often “excluded from the [official] narrative” of this moment in Georgian history. This time around, socialist realist artists are intentionally left out.

Irena Popiashvili, the dean of the Visual Arts, Architecture and Design School at Tbilisi’s Free University, said the importance of a show like this could not be understated when state museums often only focus a handful of national artists, like Georgia’s most celebrated painter Niko Pirosmani. “As an educator, it’s important for me, for example, to refer my students [to this show] and for them to be able to see the continuation of the Georgian art history, 20th century throughout and the beginning of the 21st,” she said.

The survey begins with the Thaw that followed Stalin’s death in 1953, when socialist realism remained doctrine but foreign magazines, like ARTnews and Art in America, trickled in. A pioneering figure of Abstract Expressionism in Georgia, Shura Bandzeladze saw a black-and-white reproduction of a Jackson Pollock in Art in America and took it as proof he was “on the right track,” according to Sulkhanishvili.

The risks of deviating from socialist realism were real, though. Ushangi Khumarashvili, a set designer from Kakheti’s largest city, Telavi, clashed with his director and was sent to a psychiatric hospital. On his release, he burned his earlier work and turned to abstraction. In 1974, non-conformist painter and graphic artist Otar Chkhartishvili took part in the unapproved avant-garde Bulldozer Exhibition in Moscow, which the authorities violently broke up. In Levan Chogoshvili’s painting 1924 (ca. 1980s), a dog carries a severed human hand, an image drawn from his grandmother’s account of Bolshevik executions, an episode that official Soviet histories left out. In an officially atheist country, even a return to earlier Western art traditions and the Christian themes they drew on could be equally dangerous. In 1978, Irakli Parjiani began writing out the Gospels by hand and illustrating them in the manner of medieval manuscripts, which Popiashvili described as “a revolutionary act.”

Upstairs, with perestroika in the years before the collapse of the USSR, the mood turns more hopeful. “Even though there was still censorship, even though there was the Soviet Union, there was the sense of optimism,” Sulkhanishvili said, “that something was about to happen, something was about to change.” Artists no longer worked only against the system but began building their own scene, and their canvases began to grow in scale, too. The 10th Floor group, named for its studio at the Tbilisi State Academy of Arts, later moved into a theater workshop large enough for them to realize monumental paintings. Its intellectual leader, artist and art historian Karlo Kacharava, introduced his peers to Western writers: one work here pays tribute to Allen Ginsberg. Keti Kapanadze, whom Sulkhanishvili calls Georgia’s first woman conceptual artist, plays with gender in her “Probable Need” series (1990), for which she drew over photographic self-portraits, representing herself as “Native,” “Mystery,” and “Gentleman.”

By the 1990s, war and chaos in the wake of the collapse of the USSR are answered with bitter humor. Kote Sulaberidze’s video Playing War (1994) restages the 1992–93 war in Abkhazia, a breakaway region under Russian-backed control that Georgia and most of the world regard as occupied Georgian territory, as a children’s game through a tragic yet absurd lens. Nearby, his painted portrait of former Georgian president and Soviet foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze takes its title, A Face of Caucasian Nationality (1996), from a Russian slur.

The exhibition’s final rooms turn inward, where no common movement or aesthetic prevails, though many of the artists are connected via their drawing on their personal histories. Vajiko Chachkhiani’s 2026 installation one wind after another (2026), for example, comprises recycled Georgian calfskin sewn around everyday objects, like the kind of ice cream sold during in his childhood. A metaphor for a period now gone, only the outer forms of these ice cream boxes remain.

Some artists try to contend with the unease of the recent past. Andro Eradze’s Nightvision, Limited Access (2021) is a short, poetic video of domesticated dogs abandoned during the pandemic and left to run loose, while his digital print Flow State (2025), of a taxidermy monkey in a hat, alludes to humans being locked in. In a sign of Georgian artists’ increasing international visibility, another of Eradze’s videos is now in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

The Kvareli Foundation opens at a tense moment in Georgia. A significant portion of Georgia’s art community joined the mass protests in 2023–24 against the “foreign influence” law, which requires NGOs and media groups that receive foreign funding to register as serving foreign interests. (Critics, who call it the “Russian law,” say it mirrors legislation Moscow has used to silence dissent and that it threatens Georgia’s bid to join the EU. The international watchdog group Human Rights Watch warned it would “marginalize and stifle critical voices.”)

Further protests followed the parliamentary elections in October 2024, which some claimed were fraudulent. International watchdogs describe a coordinated crackdown on dissent under the ruling Georgian Dream party, with activists and journalists facing detention, fines, and prosecution, and an ongoing lawsuit before the Constitutional Court that aims to ban five opposition parties, including the United National Movement, founded by former Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili and of which Inaishvili was a member.

This tense political situation is one many young artists now live abroad, where they also have better opportunities to show their work and sustain themselves as artists. That is partly why Sulkhanishvili did not want to shy away from including political work from the Soviet era with contemporary works that are less explicitly political. Still, she hopes visitors will see Georgia as a country still in flux. “I will be happy here if someone comes in and can see the line, how things were changing,” she said.

On the current state of the country, Sulkhanishvili strikes a different tone to the foundation’s founder; Inaishvili’s tenure as deputy chair of parliament from 2004 to 2008 is central to Georgian Dream’s ongoing lawsuit, which alleges that Saakashvili’s government is the root of the opposition parties’ wrongdoing that the ruling party hopes to root out. Inaishvili insists that people “don’t know me as a politician.”

During the opening, he reported no pressure from the government to show a certain kind of art or mount exhibitions from a specific perspective. “Every government likes when this kind of project is happening,” he said, particularly when it is privately funded. He called the overall situation “quite okay” and said artists have always been in opposition.

Sulkhanishvili is warier of the political realities of state interference, saying that while overt censorship may no longer be mandated, there is still a chilling effect that impacts the kind of art that can be made and shown in Georgia. As such, she does not plan to collaborate with state museums in order to protect the foundation’s independence. That independence rests largely on Inaishvili’s money; he has already sunk more than €25 million ($27.4 million) into the project, though funding for its continuation will be partly helped by the hotel income.

“We’re not attacking anyone. We’re just not asking anything from them,” Sulkhanishvili said, adding, “We’re not neutral in any way.” The inaugural group show’s aim to change the story of what Georgian contemporary art has been, she said, “is our statement.”

#8844. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

The HEDDphone DX is an open-back headphone that builds on the incredibly popular HEDDphone D1. It has more sub-bass and a more spiky treble, and that's a double-edged sword. Everyone will appreciate its more confident design and its improved comfort, thanks to a new Capra-created headband. But when it comes to tuning, the DX is a softer, warmer take on the lean, mean neutral D1, and I expect that'll enrage as many as it'll delight. For me, the DX is an exciting, musical set that swaps a little detail and imaging for a more fun sound. But at $400 more than the D1, and with a new Capra-created headband released for the D1 early next year, the DX runs the risk of remaining in its older sibling's shadow.

In the world of audiophile headphones and in-ear monitors (IEMs), second generations of popular products are thick on the ground. Last year the divisive Grell OAE was followed with the far better-received Grell OAE 2. Last month the ground-breaking Kiwi Ears KE4 got a second iteration.

So it would be simple to think of the new HEDDphone DX as take two of the best-selling (and my favourite open-back headphone) HEDDphone D1. Simple, but wrong.

HEDD have described it as 'the musical D1', but I think they're playing a risky game. Yes, they took on feedback from their audience, some of whom thought the D1 was a little lean and a touch too clean (not I, for the record). And they also took note of critics of the D1's unforgiving headband (yeah, that thing sucks). But instead of giving us a second take of the D1, I think they've tried to give us the HD 650 to the D1's HD 600. If that was the plan, I don't think they achieved it – but it's a fantastic failure nonetheless.

Big picture: If I were reviewing the HEDDphone DX purely on its tuning, design and comfort, it would be an easy recommendation to all. But the DX costs $400 more than the D1, so it becomes more complicated. To muddy the water further, this January HEDD plans to release the excellent DX headband as a $100 add on for the D1. That will make the D1 far more appealing – and still $300 cheaper than the DX!

So, there's plenty to consider when evaluating the new HEDDphone DX. One thing's for certain: The top spots of my list of the best-sounding wired headphones run the risk of being cluttered with HEDDphones.

Overall, the HEDDphone DX is an exciting, warm open-sounding set, with a very well extended lower frequency, and an immersive midrange. With that lower touch of warmth, it loses much of the crystal clarity of the D1, and some of that higher-end detail. But I still hear a spacious presentation with above-average imaging (the perceived placement of instruments), and enough of what makes the D1 great but with a whopping amount of sub-bass.

HEDD shared a B&K 5128 measurement of the DX with me (above), and it largely replicates what I hear. I definitely hear that slight recession in the 1-2kHz region, and an elevation in 3.5kHz. But for me, the treble's squiggly lines differ ever so slightly (all detailed below). What's clear is that HEDD want the DX to walk the tightrope of warmth and richness, while offering relaxed higher frequencies that give us detail without getting sibilant. And they nail it.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

This tuning suits diverse music genres and immersive gaming sessions, delivering clean transient speed, rich tonal body, and fatigue-free playback across dense, complex, layered multi-track studio recordings. I absolutely love it for EDM, but it's not peerless when it comes to vocal tracks, as we will see in the competition section below.

Bass: Most open-back dynamic headphones suffer from sub-bass roll-off, and that's generally been seen as a tradeoff for all that open, expansive presentation of music. The DX holds full sub-bass extension to 20Hz, smack in the middle of the new Headphones.com preference bounds on B&K 5128 measurements.

Warmth between 100Hz and 250Hz reaches the upper edge of that preference band, adding body and fullness to bass guitars and kick drums. According to HEDD's literature, the high-excursion carbon driver moves air with low - basically zero – distortion, meaning we get clean separation in the bass during complex musical passages.

Now, I don't really know how much of that is audible to the human ear. What I do know is that the bass is about as big and fun as I can enjoy before things start getting claustrophobic. You see, when bass gets overbearing, lower mids in particular can get swamped by it, and a lot of subtlety is lost. However, what the DX does to combat this is add a treble elevation around 10.5kHz, keeping things from getting too swampy. What you get is a big, detailed, but not bloated bass.

It's a tightrope, but the DX does a fantastic job walking it.

Midrange: With its bombastic bass and sneaky treble (more on that later), the mids of the DX are not really the star of the show. Not at first, at least.

But there's plenty going on. From 300Hz to 1kHz, the lower midrange sounds correct, not coloured, giving vocals, and string instruments solid weight. Then things get fun. Around 1.5 kHz there's a dip that comes across as relaxed, then a spike around 3.4kHz for me, which is only emphasised more due to the following dip around 5kHz.

All of which is to say, I can really crank the volume with the DX, and the upper midrange doesn't punish me for it. There's no shoutiness, and instead I get fatigue-free listening with coherent vocal articulation that's proportional against the rich low-end. What's more surprising, considering this rollercoaster, is that the timbre of the DX is natural sounding.

For my HEDD DX review I played them through the Luxsin X8 and the Chord Mojo 2 DAC/Amps. These pairings provided ample power delivery and headroom for the headphones, maintaining an uncoloured signal path from source to transducer. Music streamed via Spotify Lossless.

Treble is largely relaxed with the DX, trading sharp brightness for a smooth, fatigue-free approach. I hear reduced energy at 7kHz that lowers sibilance on a brightly mixed track like Sweet Old World by Lucinda Williams. That's not to say there's no bite here, but it never gets in the way of the music.

Though HEDD's B&K 5128 graph shows a narrow peak at 9-10kHz from their test pinna, for me I got clean treble extension without any glare. Strings, hi-hats, and room ambience retain a crisp texture over longer listening sessions.

I definitely got a bit of spice around 12 kHz, which isn't punishing, but brings with it some micro details, including the mouth clicks of female singers, as with Erykah Badu's Other Side of the Game.

To call the HEDDphone DX's treble dark is totally wrong. It's balanced, but edges towards modest rather than bright, and I think it'll be enjoyable to a lot of people.

I think the asking price of the HEDDphone DX is a hard sell. Yours for $1,199/£999, the DX enters a crowded open-back tier, and though I think it does well against many of them, thanks to its excellent German assembly, full part replaceability, and a five-year warranty, I think people will be expecting a truly exotic tuning for that price. That's not what the DX is about.

The HEDD DX matches the planar Audeze LCD-X at $1,199 but at half the weight, measuring 310g. It undercuts the Aune AR9000 ($1,399), HIFIMAN Arya Unveiled ($1,449), Focal Clear MG Pro ($1,490), and Sennheiser HD 800s ($1,999.95), but of course we're talking about a lot of different tunings there.

I think one of its strengths is its chic German design, and its matte black and subtle cream white does a lot to make it stand out from the crowd. The comfort is something many of the heavier contenders could learn from.

I think because the DX is not going for a risky, exotic tuning – which wins over fewer yet more ardent fans – it makes sense to compare it in detail to two mainstream, best-selling alternatives: The HEDD D1 and Sennheiser HD 650.

For those that missed it, HEDD shook the audiophile world last November with the release of the exquisitely-tuned HEDDphone D1. It was neutral, it was balanced, and for me it didn't seem to have any weaknesses at all. It wasn't warm, but it didn't come across as overly bright. It was about as lean as I can take it before things start sounding cold and clinical. But there was something about its tonal balance where its neutrality came across as rich (though I'd usually use that word to describe warmer sets). It remains my favourite over-ear, open-back headphone to date.

So, the HEDDphone DX has big shoes to fill. But ultimately, comparing them is like pitting Converse against DMs. They're trying to achieve different things... and yet, since they're coming from the same company, and at very different prices, I think the comparison is required.

The D1 is about clarity without exaggerating any part of the mix. The DX is about a good time – whacking up the bass, cranking up that 10.6kHz region to balance it... basically giving you one of the more refined V-shaped sound signatures in a high end pair of headphones.

Of course they share the same DNA when it comes to design and technology. Both headphones share thin-ply carbon drivers, though as said, HEDD positions the DX as "the experience" and the D1 as "the analyst". But that framing understates the musicality of the D1, which remains immersive and engaging despite its neutral focus.

In practice, the DX adds sub-bass weight, upper-bass warmth, a wider soundstage, and a spike up in the treble, whereas the D1 offers tighter bass and overall more focus. Then there's the price. The 'Refreshed' D1, with the new DX headband and travel case, will sell for $899/£699 in January, while the DX costs $1,199/£999.

For my tastes, and considering the price difference, the D1 remains the one I'd recommend to most people. It has more detail, and due to its neutrality presents music as a massive landscape of sound. The DX is more engaging with its bass and 10kHz shot in the arm, but it's still in its bigger brother's shadow.

However, if you find the D1 too lean, the DX could be what you want.

Both headphones share a warm-leaning, relaxed, largely fatigue-free tuning, but even though it feels neat to make a comparison between the D1 and DX with the HD 600 and HD 650, they're all actually slightly different headphones, with distinct tunings.

The Sennheiser HD 650's sub-bass rolls off from around 90Hz, and even though I think the HD 650's punchy mid-bass is criminally understated by critics, it's still easy to see someone wanting more sub bass than it offers. That's exactly what the HEDD DX does – a sub bass that extends deep to 20Hz.

Their midrange presentations are highlights for both headphones, though in subtly different ways. Both offer rich and realistic-sounding vocals and instruments, but I think the HD 650 offers slightly more forward, honeyed vocals, offering more around the 1-2kHz region than the DX, and less around 2.5kHz, giving a sense of space compared to the DX. The timbre of the HD 650 is pretty unbeatable, but the DX gives it a valiant effort.

The HD 650 is more heavy handed with the upper frequencies, which helps bring texture and grip to the mid-bass that it offers, whereas the DX takes a tamer approach to this region. For me, that makes the DX sound a touch soft, and less striking than the HD 650.

And so, I feel like the DX is actually somewhere in between the HD 600 and 650, rather than neatly comparing directly with the latter.

Though I don't believe it has any impact on the sound profile, it's still worth thinking of the different power needs. The 32ohm DX will run off anything, while the 300ohm HD 650 requires dedicated desktop amplification. Weighing 260g and costing around $500, the HD 650 also remains far more accessible, compared to the still-light 310g but slightly eye-watering $1,199, of the DX. Of course, you have to factor in the far superior build of the DX to the plastic fantastic HD 650.

If you're not going to miss the sub-bass, I'd still recommend the HD 650 over the DX. It's still my favourite out of the two. But if you know the HD 650 has a little too much spice in the upper frequencies, and you're after a soft, rich midrange – and you're willing to pay over twice the price – the HEDD DX should be on your radar.

Rated at 32ohms with a sensitivity of 100dB at 1mW, the DX is super easy to drive. I had no issues running it on my Fosi Audio DS2 dongle DAC.

Looking at price point brethren, unlike the 300ohm Sennheiser HD 800 S or the 94dB HIFIMAN Arya Unveiled, it reaches comfortable listening levels from such portable dongles and modest desktop units. A clean solid-state DAC and amplifier with low output impedance gives you excellent driver control, keeping the DX's elevated sub-bass articulate even during dynamic peaks.

The HEDDphone DX gets 10/10 for build and comfort. It really does excel in these areas, and I feel that this should be the new standard at this price point.

At 310g, it undercuts most rivals in its price point on weight. A built-in soft, silky suspension strap, designed by the king of headband comfort Capra Audio, is as good as it gets, distributing the weight across your head. We also get updated, super soft velour ear pads.

Clamp force feels firm on initial wear and may bother listeners sensitive to that, though it was fine for me across many hours of music and gaming sessions.

I also love the subtle matte charcoal metal finish, and updated indented metal mesh around the outer-ear. Add to that subtle white patterns on the outer-ear, making the HEDD logo come through, and you've got a very pretty pair of headphones here.

For $1,199, I'm glad that the DX comes with modular, user-replaceable parts and a five-year warranty. If the tuning is for you, you can expect this headphone to bring you joy for many, many years to come. Excellent work HEDD!

If you've read this review in full, you'll know it's no puff piece – I've made it clear where I think the HEDD DX is lacking. For example, it's less rich and detailed than the cheaper D1. Its above average timbre still doesn't compete with Sennheiser's HD 650, 20 years its senior and a third of its cost. For a sophisticated V-shape tuning, I think its $1,199/£999 price is steep and confusing.

So why 4.5 stars out of 5? Because the two headphones I've compared to the DX are two of my favourite headphones, and as close to perfect as I've heard.

Taken by itself, I think the DX offers exquisite build and comfort, and sounds fantastic. That half star deduction is because of its price. It's priced so much higher than the (in my opinion) better D1. That's confusing to me. Make them the same price, at least! Make it competitive, HEDD!

If you prefer a little bit more warmth, a far more forceful lower end and less overall clarity up top, then I could imagine that you'd prefer the DX to the D1. But until the HEDDphone DX dips under $1,000, I'm going to find it hard to recommend over the D1.

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. #8842. Frieze Los Angeles Lines Up 102 Exhibitors for 2027 Edition

Frieze Los Angeles has named the 102 exhibitors that will participate in its upcoming 2027 edition, scheduled to run February 25–28 at the Santa Monica Airport.

The line-up includes several returning blue-chip galleries like Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, Pace Gallery, David Zwirner, White Cube, Lisson, Gladstone, Sprüth Magers, and Thaddaeus Ropac. Galleries returning to the fair after an absence include Regen Projects, Luis De Jesus Los Angeles, Mariane Ibrahim, and Petzel.

Though several LA-based galleries and LA outposts for larger galleries have closed in the past year and a half, Frieze LA will feature 38 exhibitors with spaces in the City of Angels. They include Commonwealth and Council, Vielmetter, Marc Selwyn Fine Art, Charlie James, Night Gallery, Parker Gallery, Roberts Projects, and Make Room, which has been promoted to the main Galleries section. Related Articles This LA Exhibition of Julia Stoschek's Video Art Collection Is the City's Hottest Ticket  Nor'easter Causes Travel Delays for New York Dealers Heading to Frieze Los Angeles

“Los Angeles has many centers, each with its own history and communities, and you feel that in the work artists make here: the personal histories they draw on and the questions they’re asking about belonging and who public space is for,” Frieze Americas director Christine Messineo said in a statement. “For the city’s galleries, this is their hometown fair, a moment for the whole LA art world to show the work being made now, by artists across generations. What I love is that visitors from around the world get to experience this work right where it comes from.”

The fair will feature 22 first-time exhibitors, with 10 of them coming from the Focus section, for emerging galleries, which will be organized by Hammer curator Erin Christovale. They consist of four LA galleries, including Rajiv Menon Contemporary and House of Seiko, and six New York galleries, including Entrance, King’s Leap, and Gladwell Projects. Galleries making their debut in the main section include Gallery Wendi Norris, G Gallery, and Yehudi Hollander-Pappi.

At the fair’s entrance, visitors will be met with LA-based artist rafa esparza’s Queercancha, which will take the form of two painted adobe panels supported by a steel armature showing a scene of queer Latinxs cruising in a lowrider in the 1990s. The commission comes shortly after Hauser & Wirth announced its representation of esparza earlier this month. Additionally, his painting WeDGAF (2026) will be the main marketing image for the 2027 fair, appearing on billboards and digital screens in partnership with Orange Barrel Media, the company founded by ARTnews Top 200 Collector Pete Scantland.

“Every city brings something distinct to our network,” Frieze executive director of fairs Kristell Chadé said in a statement. “In Los Angeles, it’s how closely the visual arts sit alongside the city’s other creative industries. The fair is an opportunity for galleries and artists to connect with a collecting community that reaches into film, music, design and technology.”

#8841. South African Artist Tamlin Blake Found Dead, Germany to Restitute Archive of Nazi-Persecuted Jehovah’s Witnesses to Family, and More: Morning Links for November 24, 2026

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

WWII RECORDS RECOVERED. Germany has agreed to restitute an archive documenting Nazi persecution of Jehovah’s Witnesses, after the latter sued to recover it from Dresden’s Military History Museum, reports The New York Times. An amicable settlement finalized on November 20 concludes a years-long dispute about the rightful ownership of 31 documents and files related to the arrest and murder of the Kusserow family, who were Jehovah’s Witnesses. The archive in question “represents an invaluable part of the Witnesses’ cultural heritage and shines a light on the often overlooked abuses the group faced during World War II,” the Kusserow family stated. But Falls Short of Estimates, and More: Morning Links for November 19, 2026

IN MEMORIAM. The artist and curator Tamlin Blake was killed in her home in Riebeek West, north of Cape Town, South Africa, and a suspect has been arrested, reported local media 2 Oceans Vibe. Blake’s body was found on November 22. “The attacker took several items before [he] fled,” said a spokesperson for the Western Cape regional police. The victim’s smartphone tracking device helped locate her stolen belongings, among items thought to have been worn by the attacker. The locally celebrated artist was also chief curator at Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based organization that supports artists, helping them find opportunities to earn income, exhibit, and develop their practice, according to the website. Blake used textiles, found materials, and other mixed media, most recently consisting of tapestries woven from recycled hand-spun newspaper. “A prominent aspect of Blake’s work is her fascination with materials and manipulating new mediums in ways which take them past the merely decorative or prosaic. She was instrumental in developing beading techniques which are now used by various South African artists,” states her website.

A new lawsuit has been filed against the Trump administration to restore panels about George Washington’s stance on slavery and the nine people he enslaved while president, formerly displayed in Philadelphia’s President’s House monument. [Philly Voice]

Lévy Gorvy Dayan is bringing a Willem de Kooning priced at $32 million to Art Basel Miami Beach next week. [Artnet News]

After being featured in a Spanish television program about incredible archaeological discoveries by locals, an unearthed Roman mosaic was simply abandoned in the middle of a field, to the surprise of archaeologists. [El País]

Sotheby’s withdrew a Wade Guyton artwork estimated at $1 million to $1.5 million from its November 17 Contemporary Day Auction in New York because it was allegedly a fake, according to an unnamed source. [Artnet News]

Inconsistent requirements for and implementation of publicly supported artist housing around the US threaten the longevity and success of such initiatives. [The Art Newspaper]

FOOD FOR THOUGHT. About fifteen years ago, when Laila Gohar started making massive sculptures out of butter, she was something of an outlier, though the surrealists, Salvador Dalí in particular, had long looked at food as a playful window into the absurdity of daily life. In the Middle Ages, feasting royals were also known to host bacchanalian demonstrations of edible bounty turned into veritable sculptures. Now, according to The Guardian, Gohar is part of a trending wave of artists who use food as both main course and main medium. “I am interested in the rituals around eating and gathering, and in the way an ordinary thing can become something strange or theatrical when you change its scale, material or context,” said Gohar. “Food is one of the materials I work with, but I don’t really think of what I do as being separated into food, art, or design. They all feed into each other.”

Bonfire Studios' Nate Bowden on putting pink into dark fantasy and designing characters you can recognise mid-battle.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A lot is going on in Arkheron. Bonfire Studios' competitive multiplayer game drops players into a dark fantasy world where teams battle through an ever-changing Tower, collecting equipment and abilities as they fight. It's fast and chaotic, which creates a challenge for the art direction: how do you make a game look beautiful when players barely have time to take in what's on screen?

Built in Unity, Arkheron answers by putting gameplay at the centre of its visual identity. That has shaped the rotating isometric camera, the colourful character designs, and how weapons, animation, and sound communicate information during combat.

I spoke to Nate Bowden, art director at Bonfire Studios, about Arkheron's world, its characters and the visual language that holds them together.

Asked for the first image that made the team feel "this is Arkheron", Bowden doesn't offer one. "I don't know if there was a single piece of art that suddenly made everything click for everyone all at once," he says. "I think Arkheron's visual identity has been something we've discovered and refined over time."

The look grew up alongside the mechanics. "The IP and its look and feel started in parallel with 'finding the fun' in its gameplay and design," he says. "Once the Arkheron that we know and love now started to take shape, art followed suit, and the team started making choices that enhanced the gameplay experience rather than just looked cool for its own sake."

If he had to name a single visual idea, it would be the camera. "It would have to be the camera and the choice to make it isometric and also one that rotated around the player," he says. "That helped inform so many decisions on where we should put time and effort."

It also shaped how the team approached dark fantasy. "I think there's a misconception that dark fantasy has to be relentlessly dark, grim, or oppressive," Bowden says. One of the team's guiding ideas has been a world that's "hauntingly beautiful", and he thinks they've shown that "you can have environments and characters that have a broad palette of colours and still feel melancholic, mysterious, and dangerous."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

For another game that resists photorealism, read how Blades of Fire flew in the face of modern video game aesthetics, taking a painterly, high-contrast route.

His example is the rework of Dahla, the game's deadly dancer. The Eternals at the time already resembled today's lineup, but their designs were more detailed, and the palettes were, in his words, "very clamped and constrained". Then came the challenge. "The challenge I put in front of the team was 'we are going to have pink in the game.'"

"In the end I believe that she turned out not only more vibrant and colourful, but also even more threatening than her original design, which tended to disappear in the shadows," he says. The wider cast now has a broad range of colours, and the payoff is practical. "When you are in those crazy fights, it is so much easier to differentiate the characters from one another from colour alone."

"Oh man, I could answer this question forever," reflects Bowden when the focus turns to the story behind the Tower.

The short version: the Tower is an afterlife inhabited by Echoes, entities that were once human in the living world. They're trapped in an endless cycle by their own unfinished business, as the Tower builds itself up and then essentially resets. Everything in Arkheron, from someone's appearance to a piece of furniture, is formed from someone's memory, and none of it needs to be accurate. "They're imperfect recollections, shaped by emotion, experience; all rooted in that unfinished business," he says.

A type of Echo called Builders creates the levels. "Their memories and unfinished business are so strong and profound that they have, in a way, contaminated the tower architecturally."

"We want the world to feel like it has a history, even when you don't fully understand that history when you begin," Bowden says. Their stories will be revealed as people play, "which is something we can't wait to share."

Building maps that work as both fantasy spaces and competitive arenas can be difficult, but Bowden is direct in how the art team approached it. "One of the principles I feel most strongly about is that gameplay has to come first. We can create the most beautiful environment imaginable, but if it makes the game harder to understand or less enjoyable to play, we haven't done our job as developers."

The camera can orbit the action, and players are often fighting several opponents, so they need to read their surroundings almost instantly. That means thinking about silhouettes, landmarks, navigable space and how much visual information players are being asked to process. Bowden doesn't see those as limits. "Quite the opposite; they force us to make stronger decisions."

Where Arkheron's character work puts its emphasis surprised me. "A lot more emphasis is ultimately put on the items vs. the character's bodies themselves," Bowden says. "That's not to say that we don't put a lot of love and attention there too, but as a player it's more important that you quickly recognise what that enemy player has equipped, because that's 100% going to impact how you respond in combat."

So the items get every tool the team has. "Yes, of course we think about colour and shape, but we really live and die by the emphasis we put on bespoke audio, animation, and VFX." He gives three examples:

"I can literally hear you from offscreen and know when you have switched to Ravah's Crossbow. When you attack with Dahla's weapons, you move like a dancer because you are embodying her with her items. When you use Karriv's abilities, you are literally setting the playspace on fire."

The characters themselves have to work at two scales. Up close, they should be "beautiful, detailed, and full of personality". In play, they're seen from an elevated camera, surrounded by other players, abilities and effects. "At that distance, a lot of traditional character detail simply disappears. What remains is silhouette, proportion, movement, sound, and colour," he says. Because players can combine equipment and abilities in different ways, "we're not just designing a fixed cast of characters. We're creating a visual language that helps players understand what they're encountering."

When thinking about the creative process, Bowden uses the Eternals as an example, whose items are driven by gameplay. New ones usually start from a fun gameplay prototype. Sometimes the trigger is a narrative need, and sometimes it's a drawing from the skin design process that "we all just agree needs to be flushed out and developed as an Eternal."

A small group works out what's missing. If the starting point is a combat prototype, that means working out who the person was in the living world, what their unfinished business was, and what they looked like while alive. Then a larger strike team, with someone from each discipline, hears the pitch of the backstory and abilities. The team gives them "as few visuals as possible", usually just a living-world drawing, and lets them decide how the character will look, sound and move. "That kickoff pitch and backstory is the North Star that we keep referring back to throughout the process."

"I think the best cosmetics do more than simply make a character look different," Bowden says. "They give players another way to express themselves, and ideally they reveal something interesting about the world." Every cosmetic reflects something about who that person was in the living world, an area of the Tower, or "an ecology or culture that has developed over aeons in this afterlife."

The team also decided early that although cosmetics are often designed as cohesive sets, players can mix and match between them. "Arkheron is ultimately about cool combinations of items and cosmetics are no exception," he says. "We've already got some awesome and unanticipated cosmetic combos that our team has put together during our playtests."

Identity, memory and transformation are already central to the world, which he says makes exploring different looks for a character feel natural. "I'll give a funny example just to illustrate that," he says. Someone in the living world may have been a baker, and the team could design a baker-themed Echo. But in the lore, that baker may have spent a thousand years in the Tower, mostly in one of the Builders' areas, say the Archivist's level. "That same Echo may now totally take on the look of the level they inhabit vs. what they do or don't remember from the living world."

Readability sets the limits. "A cosmetic should never leave another player confused about what they're fighting or what's happening on screen," Bowden says. He describes an emote for the Armored Swan skin where you pop angelic wings. "I would have loved to have you fly or float in the air when you use it, but that would be terrible for gameplay and add a lot of player confusion." Size is off the table too, as he says, "I can't have a character skin that is two times larger than the other skins because our hitboxes need to stay consistent for combat and we wouldn't want a player confused for an enemy NPC."

"One of the most important things we keep beating the drum on is that visual quality isn't necessarily about putting more things on screen," Bowden says. "Often, it's about knowing what to leave out. I like to think of polish as an act of conscious removal."

Combat is crowded, and there's a natural temptation to make every character, ability, effect and environment as spectacular as possible. "I think that's a trap that happens when you look at any one of those facets in a vacuum," he says. What guards against it is that the whole team plays every day. "My favourite thing about the culture of the whole Arkheron team is that we all play the game every day. That forces all of us to look at everything in context and as a whole and not as one detail over on your own desktop."

That leads to a set of questions he keeps asking. "What should the player notice first? What's important to gameplay? What can remain atmospheric or understated?" Lighting gives environments mood and personality, but it also has to support character and combat readability. Visual effects should make abilities feel powerful and satisfying while letting players understand what's happening and respond.

On PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, the goal is simple. "One of our goals has been to make Arkheron feel like Arkheron regardless of where you're playing it." The game was built from the start to feel great on controller as well as mouse and keyboard, which affects performance, readability, responsiveness, and how much information players see.

Platforms have different technical constraints, so the team has to decide where to spend its resources. "I think there's an important difference between preserving every individual visual detail and preserving the artistic intent," he says. The team wants to deliver the atmosphere, character identities, combat clarity, and overall feeling of the world consistently. "And frankly, being disciplined about performance and readability often makes the game better for everyone, regardless of platform. Speaking for myself, the aspect that excites me the most is being able to play with my friends regardless of our hardware of choice."

"I hope their first reaction is curiosity," Bowden says. A video, and especially a screenshot, is likely to give the wrong impression of how the game plays. "You might see that isometric camera and think it's a point-and-click game, or you may see that it is PVP and think it's going to play like a MOBA. It won't." The art, the lore and the gameplay, he says, "are familiar ingredients that are combined in a really original way."

It's a game where you're constantly learning: discovering equipment, trying ability combinations, figuring out how to cooperate with teammates, and outplaying opponents. "There's something incredibly satisfying about the moment when all of that starts to click." The art's job is to make that journey feel exciting and intuitive, with a world that captures the imagination, characters and abilities that make you feel powerful, and visual feedback that explains why you succeeded or failed.

His hope for the first hour: "If a player finishes their first hour thinking, 'I have no idea how good I could get at this, but I really want to find out,' I think we've accomplished something pretty special."

#8839. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

#8838. Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface

Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an important part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos launched earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the company’s website.

#8837. A Minimalist, a Maximalist, and 30 Years of Friendship

Two person shows are taking over the art world, with galleries doubling as matchmakers, mostly pairing dead artists with market darlings. But of course, nothing beats conversation between two old friends.

At Gladstone in New York this fall, that’s just what you’ll get, with a new show from British artists Sarah Lucas and Cerith Wyn Evans titled “Je Pense.”

The two talked to Art in America about the exhibition, and their 30-year friendship, below. Related Articles Julia Stoschek Collection to Celebrate 20 Years with 'Selfish in Bed' Exhibition and Düsseldorf Reopening Sarah Lucas Wins New Museum's $400,000 Sculpture Prize

You two have been friends since the ’90s. How’d you meet?

Cerith Wyn Evans: I never can answer questions like that because I never remember. We were probably both drunk somewhere.

CWE: I do remember hearing of you. I was close with a painter at the time, Angus Cook, and I’d ask him things like “What’s Gary Hume like?,” all this kind of stuff. Later I quipped, “We should really be talking about his girlfriend, a much better artist. She’s called Sarah Lucas.”

Angus said he had met you once: He knocked on the door and you answered—allegedly!—and he said “Hi, are you Gary?” and you replied “NO.” He told me “Oh my God, She’s incredible!”

SL: I remember meeting Angus at a party Matthew Marks gave for Gary, maybe that’s where I met you. A lot of things were happening at that time, around 1990; something was burgeoning. I met a lot of people then that became friends for life.

You can’t make new old friends! When I saw that you two were showing together, I admit my first thought was: a minimalist and a maximalist walk into a bar.

CWE: Who’s who? [laughs] I’m certainly the maximalist.

Ha. All that’s to say, at first glance, I thought of you two as having quite different sensibilities, but they really do converge beautifully in the gallery. I know you’ve wanted to show together for quite a while.

SL: We’ve kicked the notion around for a long time, but it was more of a mythic show, something we might do some day—it wasn’t about whether we ever did it or not.

CWE: I think if you really really care how another person thinks, if you don’t take them for granted, you imagine your dialogue… but also the distance between our work allows a certain level of respect. Nancy Spector invited us, and really, the show’s a kind of hologram that Nancy has somehow… well, she’s the Wizard of Oz.

So the differences help. Okay, I have to ask about the burnt-out car in the gallery, obviously.

CWE: For me, that’s the fulcrum of the entire exhibition because it’s so brutal. It’s like a black hole in the middle of the entire thing, and a vortex that everything sucks everything else in, or spits it all out, or something. It’s phenomenal, extraordinary and also this quotidian tragedy, a very pure readymade. Sarah bought it at an auction, already burnt. I guess weird death perverts buy these things.

SL: I have no idea who would buy these things… apart from us.

Did you make the work in tandem and plan it out, or just bring things together at the end? I love how Sarah’s sculpture makes Cerith’s tower feel very phallic.

CWE: No, we’ve just always been very erotic, very horny. See, this is the maximalist in me coming out.

SL: Besides, things are always different when you get them somewhere anyway.

Have you guys been like doing studio visits and giving each other feedback over the years?

CWE: No no no. It’s organic. It’s natural. It’s spiritual. We’re not really that organized.

SL: That’s probably why we like each other. We get on because we don’t have that kind of mindset that would make us, I don’t know, strategic.

I’m just thinking about a lot of younger artists who are working hard to sustain creative community. I don’t know if you have thoughts or advice for them.

SL: No one takes advice, do they? Though I will say, younger artists should be in more group shows. When you’re young, you’re so eager to have your moment in the spotlight.

Has your friendship ever felt competitive?

SL: We just aren’t really strategic like that. I’m not a jealous person by nature. I’m just in my own world, making work.

CWE: I think it’s sad when people compare themselves and are concerned with who’s more famous or younger or richer.

Do you talk about art together then, or other stuff?

CWE: I don’t think I talk about anything else. But it depends what how you by mean “Art.” I’m obsessed by creativity more than much art with a price tag.

#8835. Dora Maar’s Paris Apartment Is For Sale, Picasso Wall Drawings and All

In this quiet, 17th-century Parisian apartment on rue de Savoie in the 6th arrondissement, strange-looking insects appear to be climbing up the middle of the living room wall near the chimney. But these 15 or so critters—spiders, ants, and cockroaches—are actually drawn and carefully protected by glass coverings.

That’s because they were made by none other than Pablo Picasso, once a regular visitor to this home, where his lover, the artist Dora Maar, lived from 1946 until she died in 1997. The abode, along with the Picasso drawings on the wall, is now for sale, listed for the lump sum of €2.85 million (about $3.1 million), reports Le Parisien. How’s that for a dinner party icebreaker? Related Articles Christie's Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons's Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie's, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso

Picasso used to call Maar “ma puce,” which literally means “my flea” and is used as an endearing term in French for “my sweetheart.” It is believed Picasso’s drawings were a playful pun on his nickname for Maar, per the apartment’s current owner, identified only as Ida. “They give it a history,” she added.

All the wall artworks have been officially recognized by the Picasso Administration, which manages the artist’s estate, and oversees a committee that catalogs his works.

Many may know Maar (1907–97) as the famous figure Picasso depicted in many paintings over the course of their seven-year relationship, including his “Weeping Woman” series, and another portrait of her from 1943 that sold for $37 million in 2025, quadrupling its estimate. Yet Maar herself has been belatedly recognized for her own paintings and photographs that contributed to the Surrealist movement’s heyday in Paris from the 1920s to the 1940s.

The 1,600-square-foot apartment’s well-lit rooms, large windows, and high ceilings do fit an artistic sensibility, said the owner. With two bedrooms, an office, kitchen, and the famous Picasso-drawn living room, the Maar’s former home also boasts 13th-century petrified wooden beams from a former mansion that was converted into the apartment building.

Future owners of Maar’s apartment will also be able to hop over to the Louvre and the Centre Pompidou, right across the Seine River. Then again, if the urge to see art by a modern master strikes them, they won’t even need to leave their living room.

#8834. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!
