#8813. the architecture of waiting: reimagining train stations as places for public life

from libraries and community kitchens to cultural venues and sports facilities, new projects are rethinking how airports and train stations can accommodate public life beyond travel.

Train stations and airports are places where people spend a lot of time, but rarely by choice. Most are designed to keep passengers moving, with waiting areas, stores and services filling the hours between arrival and departure. Some recent projects are taking a different approach, bringing libraries, exhibition spaces, sports facilities, and community services into transport hubs. In Warsaw, Seoul, and Rovereto, stations are being used for things that have little to do with catching a train.

For many people, the station is part of a routine, whether it means passing through on the way to work, waiting for a connection, or meeting someone before heading elsewhere. Despite this constant use, there is little to do there beyond the journey itself. A library, a public reading room, or a space for workshops may seem an unlikely addition to a station, but a number of projects are finding ways to make these uses part of the daily commute.

Historically, railway stations have served as important civic buildings, marking the entrance to a city and bringing together people from different backgrounds. Over time, however, security requirements, commercial development, and the growing scale of transportation networks have shaped them around circulation and passenger services. Waiting is mostly perceived as a waste of time rather than an opportunity to create a different kind of urban experience.

In Warsaw, Poland, a new library inside Kondratowicza metro station offers an alternative perspective. Designed by GK-Atelier, led by Grzegorz Kłoda, Metroteka opened in September 2025 with around 16,000 books across a 150-square-meter space. The library includes separate reading areas for adults and children, shared workspaces, laptop loans, and room for public events. A hydroponic garden, where plants grow without soil or natural sunlight, also introduces an educational element focused on subjects such as sustainability and food production.

A similar approach appears in Shanghai, where X-Lighthouse opened inside the city’s South Railway Station in August 2025. The 400-square-meter reading space offers books on literature, architecture, art, local culture, and travel, alongside a dedicated area for children, giving passengers a place to engage with something other than their departure time.

Other projects take this idea further, treating railway stations as places that can support the needs of the surrounding community, including people who may not use the train at all. In Rovereto, northern Italy, the Station for Transformation initiative thinks of new ways in which underused rooms in the historic railway station can contribute to local life. Developed with the municipality, railway infrastructure operator RFI, and the community group La Foresta, the project builds on spaces that have already been reused for coworking, meetings, and a community kitchen. Activities include cooking classes, cultural events, and initiatives that bring residents together around environmental and social issues.

The wider project aims to turn the station into a public hub focused on climate change, biodiversity, and local heritage, proposing spaces for collaboration, education, and experimentation, including a climate-focused community kitchen and areas where residents, researchers, and local organizations can develop ideas together. The initiative makes use of rooms at the station that would otherwise remain empty. It is an example of how the future of transportation architecture might involve rethinking what already exists, as much as building something new.

A related approach is taking shape across smaller towns in Italy through the Stazioni del Territorio program, promoted by railway group FS Italiane. Completed projects in Popoli Vittorito, Matelica, and Urbisaglia-Sforzacosta in 2024, followed by further stations in 2025, introduce public services into railway buildings and previously unused areas. Depending on the location, these include medical consultations, support from the Italian Red Cross, community services, coworking, and training facilities. The project is particularly relevant in smaller communities, where access to public services can be limited and a railway station may already occupy a central position in local life. At Popoli Vittorito, for example, the station houses medical services and screening activities.

Public life does not have to mean large cultural institutions or permanent community facilities. Sometimes, a smaller intervention can change the way people use a familiar place. In April 2026, Vilnius Railway Station introduced Sun Hall, a 320-square-meter multifunctional venue designed by 2L Architects & Engineers. The flexible interior can host exhibitions, concerts, conferences, and creative gatherings, with curtains allowing the space to be rearranged for different events. Located within the operating station, it offers another reason for residents and visitors to enter the building. The project is also the first step in a wider program to introduce similar cultural spaces at railway stations in other Lithuanian cities.

In Seoul, South Korea, the idea extends into recreation and everyday fitness. The city’s Fun Station initiative transforms underused areas of metro stations into facilities for activities that would normally take place elsewhere. Runner Station, which opened at Yeouinaru station in May 2024, provides lockers, changing rooms, and spaces for stretching, alongside running classes and community programs. Further facilities have followed, including a fitness space at Ttukseom station and a park-golf facility at Meokgol station. The program reflects the particular relationship between these stations and nearby recreational areas, including the Han River parks. In August 2026, the initiative expanded into culture with K-Culture Station, an underground venue between City Hall and Euljiro 1(il)-ga stations, using a previously closed space for exhibitions and immersive cultural experiences.

These projects show that train stations and airports can accommodate activities well beyond their usual functions. Yet adding new functions does not necessarily make a place more public. A cultural venue inside a transport hub may still be accessible only to ticketed passengers, open for a few hours a day, or reserved for visitors who can afford to pay. An airport lounge, for instance, might offer comfortable seating and somewhere to work, but its purpose and access are quite different from those of a public library or community center.

What really matters, then, is who gets to take part. Can someone come in to read a book without having to buy anything? Can local residents visit an exhibition without catching a train? Can people use the space without being expected to spend money or move on? These questions become particularly important when stations are considered part of the public space, rather than facilities serving passengers alone. Their relationship with the surrounding neighborhood depends, in part, on whether they welcome the people who live and work nearby, as well as those passing through.

#8812. Upside-down cantilever cracks open timber hotel by BIG

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.

Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, BIG designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.

Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s new Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.

The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.

The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,

“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a new development,” BIG partner Sören Grünert said.

“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.

“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”

The hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.

BIG used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.

The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.

Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.

BIG also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.

It's our top pick for multi-platform gaming.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We've spent a lot of time tracking Nintendo Switch 2 Black Friday deals here at Creative Bloq since the console's a favourite among many of our team. But Black Friday offers treats for gamers on other platforms too. One of the most appealing has to be 28% off the GameSir Super Nova, now $49.99 $35.99 at Amazon.

This is a record discount on a versatile wireless controller that we gave a five-star review when it was released last year. It's compatible with multiple platforms: PC, Android and iOS ad well as Nintendo Switch, and our reviewer reckons it has certain advantages over Nintendo's own Pro Controller.

For PC gamers, there's also 20% off the wonderful GameSir G7 Pro 8K controller, which is simply excellent.

We love the GameSir Super Nova for its wide compatibility, sturdy build and sleek design. As well as serving for PC, iOS and Android, it's a strong alternative to the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller if you want Hall Effect sticks and triggers, back buttons, multi-platform support, and a lower price tag.

This Aimlabs collab from GameSir features the former's iconic cyan colour scheme and logo and a 8000Hz polling rate over both wired and 2.4G wireless, which is the fastest we've tested on a wireless controller, eliminating any lag.

The Super Nova oozes quality for a surprisingly affordable price, with a solid build and a range of colour combinations. It uses Hall Effect sensors to prevent stick drift and improve durability. It has two mappable rear buttons, analog triggers with travel locks/stoppers, swappable ABXY face buttons, and a magnetic faceplate. And it costs less than the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller while still supporting gyro motion controls and up to a 1000Hz polling rate

A switch next to the RT/LT triggers swaps between a short or long trigger travel, short for instant response and long for greater level of control, allowing you to switch between them for games that require fast reflexes from the triggers and ones that benefit from more modulated throttle and brake response. Combine that with the little M button on the front, and you've got yourself an additional hair-trigger mode too.

As it's a Switch-compatible controller, it had to have a good gyro for motion control, and the six-axis gyro does indeed works very well for steering, swinging and flinging on-screen objects.

Multi-platform compatibility works across Nintendo Switch/Switch 2, PC, and mobile devices via Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless dongle, or USB, and it comes with a charging stand (which can house the wireless dongle) and a physical power switch to avoid accidental battery drain.

The G7 Pro 8K's sticks use 'Mag-Res' technology for greater input precision, an the trigger stops are dual-mode, so you can switch between Hall Effect analog triggers and micro-switch triggers. The former is ideal for racing, the latter for RPGs and hectic shooters.

In addition to the remappable back buttons, there are extra L5 and R5 buttons next to left and right triggers, also remappable. Our reviewer found the 6-axis gyroscope offers good motion control, and the rumble motors are immersive and nuanced rather than thunderous and distracting.

#8809. Extra Skin? 9 Exercises for A Sagging Neck

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

We’re not in love with the term “turkey neck” — it’s just extra skin.

If you don’t want to learn to love the extra chin you’re in (though we wish you would!), you can perform some exercises that may tighten your neck muscles.

Though some swear these moves work, there’s no research backing them up, and they can’t zap away extra flowy skin.

Instead, they’re more likely to help strengthen the muscles underneath loose neck skin. Unfortunately, skin removal is usually accomplished with more intense methods, like surgery.

However, these popular neck exercises are simple enough for a test drive and may help tone your neck muscles naturally.

Exercise may be possible to tighten up a turkey neck, but it doesn’t eliminate loose skin like surgery or lasers.

Yes. Certain cosmetic products and procedures — especially surgery — improve loose neck skin the best. These include surgical neck lifts, lasers, Botox, and certain neck creams.

Surgery and other cosmetic methods for turkey neck can offer impressive results.

Are you not into cosmetic procedures or surgery? Neck-toning exercises and facial yoga movements may offer some improvement. However, loose skin is generally not tightened naturally.

Loose neck skin is normal (and honestly v common).

Still, these simple moves may result in toned neck muscles. Just be careful so you don’t wind up with an actual pain in the neck. If you can, it’s best to chat with a healthcare professional first.

CD Projekt Red staff and Naughty Dog's Michael Barclay are among the developers reacting to GTA 6's record 99 Metascore.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 has been out for less than a week, and it isn't just players and critics who are losing their minds. I gave it 5/5 in my GTA 6 review, and it holds a 99 Metascore, tying Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game ever. As more people play and see more of Leonida, other game developers (those who really know what's what) are lining up to say they're a bit rattled.

The most dramatic reaction I've read came from Igor Sarzyński, creative director on Cyberpunk 2. Reported on Shift Delete, he posted on Bluesky on Saturday evening, two days after launch, and started with "GTA VI-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real", then called it "probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history" and "a technological and creative miracle".

He joked that Cyberpunk 2 was cancelled and he was off to sweep leaves in his garden.

As our sister site GamesRadar+ covered, Sarzyński isn't the only CD Projekt Red game dev impressed. Joint CEO Michał Nowakowski called the game a masterpiece and said it's "unbelievably hard" to achieve what Rockstar has. Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Paweł Sasko called it a "generational banger". Witcher 4 director Sebastian Kalemba said he'd love to lose a whole weekend to it, although he's busy hunting monsters for now.

@RockstarGames created a masterpiece that I am planning to explore in the coming weeks and months. Massive congratulations to the whole team who worked on the game. It is unbelievably hard to achieve what you just did. Hats off to all of youNovember 19, 2026

Over at Naughty Dog, Michael Barclay, who has 19 years in the industry and is working on Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, said GTA 6 looks to him like "a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child".

Push Square picked up on how Barclay was impressed by the lighting specifically, which he explained is mostly dynamic, yet he says it looks as good as, if not better than, most baked lighting. That's a big deal in an open world where the weather and time of day never stop changing.

Tim Soret of Odd Tales (The Last Night) joined the thread, saying he can't work out how Rockstar gets so many draw calls, hair simulations and volumetric lights running at once.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

I’ve made video games for 19 years and GTA VI appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child.November 20, 2026

None of this surprises anyone who's seen how Rockstar builds its world. As I reported earlier, Rockstar's art team designs buildings by imagining who actually lives in them. And then there's the fact that the animators spend months on small details, like how Lucia opens a door with her hip in a natural way when her hands are full.

VP of art Miriam Bellard says they ask whether a place is messy or tidy, and "what is their taste?" The range runs from industrial and scruffy to decadent and dangerous.

So it seems the people who made GTA 6 are as stunned as everyone else by what they've achieved. As GamesRadar+ reported, Rockstar production coordinator Navya Manaswitha reacted to the reviews by saying she's "truly grateful to be a part of this masterpiece".

I've already argued Rockstar has bucked the AI trend in how it made the game, and GTA 6 is proof that human creativity is still the most impressive technology we have. It seems most game devs agree.

#8807. HOFF transforms its madrid flagship with a festive explosion of color by studio wanda

inside its flexible 600 m² flagship on madrid’s velázquez street, hoff merges footwear retail, specialty coffee, and art with a sculpted holiday installation by studio wanda.

mariana rodrigues November 24, 2026 4 min

HOFF opened a 600 m² flagship on Madrid’s Velázquez street, and it turns out they are providing way more than just sneakers. Built by architecture studio El Departamento to shift on demand, the fluid layout brings together a retail showroom, gallery, and café designed for rotating exhibitions, workshops, and community meetups. Its latest transformation arrives just in time for the holidays, as Barcelona-based Studio Wanda steps in with an immersive, custom Christmas installation named ‘Velvet Firebloom’. Conceived as a reflection of HOFF’s ongoing exploration of color, materiality, and creative expression, the intervention turns the flagship into an evolving space for design collaborations and cultural experiences.

The flagship guides visitors through a series of rooms that open into a central gathering hub. It captures the brand‘s vision for a dynamic retail concept where shopping, art installations, food, and cultural events naturally collide, creating a platform for creative expression that steps outside the shoebox. Inside, travertine marble, custom furniture, and theatrical spotlights team up to treat sneakers like fine art.

Titled ‘Velvet Firebloom’, the holiday takeover by Studio Wanda freezes the split-second pop of a firework mid-air, sparing visitors the loud bang while keeping all the visual spectacle. Working under the concept of Explosion de Color, the studio unfolded sharp geometric lines that erupt outward from a single focal point, blooming into sculpted paper planes that animate the entire room with tactile gradients. This rush of folded paper spills straight out toward Madrid’s streets, transforming HOFF’s storefront into an uninterrupted sculpture.

Inside, the chromatic burst weaves naturally through the entrance architecture, winding past the travertine display blocks of The Stage and framing the SNEAKS café. Just past it sits The Gallery, where Moisés Nieto curates contemporary design pieces and art publications.

Beyond the installation, Velázquez 37 operates as a dynamic hub built to bring Madrid’s design community together. Upstairs, The Work-Shop hosts talks, workshops, and dinners around a 20-meter folding table, joined by footwear customization at The Charm Bar and intimate gatherings inside The Attic, uniting retail with cultural discovery under one roof.

#8806. "All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

The beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the new Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

That last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the big deal.

A both bigger and smaller issue is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences

That is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

The architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

In recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same issues that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

To be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility issues – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many users, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Hunters Point Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers

That leaves only a deeper issue, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once said, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

#8805. Nopales Benefits: Why You Might Add Cactus to Your Diet

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.)

Nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

Older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

You can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:

If you’re new to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

#8803. can le corbusier’s last building be disassembled and shipped?

some 22,000 screws hold together the pavillon le corbusier's prefabricated steel frames in zurich, yet its concrete ramp, staircase, and legacy make relocation near-impossible.

annalise kamegawa November 24, 2026 9 min

The Pavillon Le Corbusier on Lake Zurich is the last completed building by the late French-Swiss architect. Made of glass and steel, it is his only building to have been constructed in this format, and it has a tricky history of ownership, construction, and maintenance. Having been approached by the gallerist Heidi Weber, who went on to represent his non-architectural projects, the project was made possible by her tenacity, his experimentation, and a fifty-year land lease from the city.

After its opening in 1967, the pavilion enjoyed decades on that grassy plot. When the half-century period came to a close, Weber, who had a contract stating that she could take everything that was allowed to be moved, packed up the lighting, art, seating, and tables. In conversation with designboom, Christian Brändle, director of the Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, which now manages the Pavilion, mentions a popular rumor in the city: ‘There was always a bit of a difficult relationship between Heidi Weber and the city,’ he begins, before elaborating on the gossip that claims ‘she tried to dismantle the building, which is technically not really possible because of [the Pavilion’s] ramp and the staircase is made of concrete.’

above and banner shows Pavillon Le Corbusier, 2019, Zürich | image by Umberto Romito & Ivan Šuta, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich/ZHdKPavillon Le Corbusier, 1st floor, 2019, Zürich | image by Umberto Romito & Ivan Šuta, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich/ZHdK

In order to claim the building as part of the dispute, it has been said that she tried to take the Pavillon Le Corbusier apart and bring it with her alongside the other interior furnishings. The idea that this was possible comes from the fact that, as Brändle mentions, ‘basically, the building pretends to be prefabricated. Of course, all the frames were screwed together with around 22,000 screws on the building site… but it would be absolutely impossible to keep it as it is and to unscrew it and to rebuild it in another place.’

Here, in this pavilion, Weber gave the architect permission to experiment. Although it is a kind of house with a kitchen, bunker, and unrealized bedroom, it is ultimately a museum for his ideas. ‘He really assembled almost every idea he had as an architect in the pavilion,’ reflects Brändle on what would be Le Corbusier’s final project. ‘And a real key power of modernism has always been that design and architecture should come out of the machine,’ he says, referencing the popular idea of ‘houses as machines for living,’ or ‘une maison est une machine à habiter,’ in French, from his popular 1923 manifesto, Vers une architecture.

Pavillon Le Corbusier, drawing on enamel based on the lithograph “Os 2” from 1964 on the outside of its revolving door, 2025, Zürich | image by Lucas ZieglerPavillon Le Corbusier, kitchen corner, 2015, Zürich | image by Georg Aerni

Brändle cites the fallout of the First World War and how prefabricated homes became a counterpoint to the overly decorated standards of the time. ‘You would divide your architecture into elements that could be produced somewhere and then you bring it to the building site and assemble it over there.’ He goes on to say that ‘Le Corbusier was, of course, always upfront when it came to innovation,’ and wanted to implement these processes in his architecture, but had passed away before truly realizing the potential of this method. Nevertheless, he got to experiment with some of these techniques in the Pavilion, which becomes evident in the aforementioned thousands of screws and the 226 × 226 × 226 centimeter units used to construct the entire building.

The building opened on July 15, 1967, as the Centre Le Corbusier – Heidi Weber Museum. Brändle, who frequently liaises between the city of Zurich and Weber herself, who is nearly a hundred years old, speaks fondly of her wit and foresight. ‘When she visited an exhibition at the Kunsthaus Zürich, the art museum, in 1957 about Le Corbusier and his oeuvre, she decided that she will devote the rest of her professional life to the spread the ideas of Le Corbusier’s ideas.’ Although it was a grand idea, he was already regarded as a kind of ‘star-chitect’ of the period, making him a tricky man to get hold of.

Brändle recounts her cleverness, saying that she finally got hold of him when a property next to Le Corbusier’s quiet, retreat-like home, Le Cabanon, went up for sale. He remarks that ‘Corbusier was a bit nervous to get a neighbor he wouldn’t like because he was there all day. If he had some clothes, it was just a swimming suit, but nothing else because it was hot and he wanted to paint, sometimes even naked!’ To avoid having new neighbors who could disturb his peace, he went about trying to find a buyer himself. He was connected to Heidi Weber, who had already become a successful gallerist, with the idea that perhaps her clients would be interested in the villa.

In the end, Weber went to visit this Mediterranean property under the guise of helping to find a buyer and instead knocked on the architect’s door and proposed the idea of becoming his future gallerist. Though he was shocked, as he had never sold a painting before, Le Corbusier eventually agreed. Unfortunately, she sold almost none of them. ‘She decided to sell her little car, her Fiat Topolino, and she went back to Paris with all the money she had from selling the car and gave it to Corbusier, pretending she sold everything. And Corbusier was absolutely thrilled and said, well, she is a genius,’ Brändle recounts of the moment that she became one of his biggest advocates in both art and architecture.

‘That the pavilion is the only building that is turned by 45 degrees,’ says Brändle of its orientation relative to all the other homes in the neighborhood that surrounds it. ‘[The other homes] are in parallel to the street. Le Corbusier always wanted to build a house that is like the Parthenon in Athens.’ The building was constructed at an angle, but a compromise had to be made. Although the architect wanted direct access from the street, a winding path had to be built instead. ‘And Heidi was very upset [about this] because she said, you are betraying not only me, but also the ideas of Le Corbusier.’ This, alongside the land dispute and other particularities, adds to the tricky history of the architect’s last structure. Since 2019, the building has been considered the third part of the Zurich Design Museum, with the institution embarking on a major restoration of the space, which involved refinishing its sloped roof.

There is an amusing contradiction in the Pavilion’s history. A building conceived around the principles of prefabrication, assembled from modular elements and thousands of screws, has proved remarkably difficult to move. Despite its appearance as a structure that could be taken apart and reassembled elsewhere, its concrete staircase and ramp firmly anchor it to its original site. The story of Heidi Weber’s dispute with the city adds another layer to this curious history, raising questions about who gets to claim a building and what it means to preserve it. In a way, the Pavilion embodies two competing ideas of architecture: one that embraces movement, experimentation, and the possibility of relocation, and another that understands a building as inseparable from its place. Today, under the care of the Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, it remains on the lakeside plot where it was first conceived. Perhaps its greatest achievement is not that it can be moved, but that it continues to make us question why architecture has to stay put.

#8802. Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

With The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh says, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused New Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the issues that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

“I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she says has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she said.

The Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

#8801. Ultimate Guide to 4A Hair: Care Tips, Styles, and Maintenance

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

Alright, curl friends, let’s break it down. Hair type falls into four main categories:

Now, Type 4 hair is where things get seriously curly and coily. Within this category, we’ve got subtypes A, B, and C,

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Yes, 4A hair is curly and falls under the coily category. It features tight, springy curls that form an S-shape.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Love those natural curls — keep them hydrated, avoid excessive heat, and give them some nighttime TLC.

Earn Alaska miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa, Marriott Bonvoy® transfers (3:1 ratio with 5K bonus per 60K), or direct purchase during sales. Target 60,000 miles for a one-way business class ticket.

Use JAL's own award search tool to check business class availability before contacting Alaska. Search 331 days out from your desired travel date. Look for flights showing "Partner Award" availability on JAL's calendar.

Verify your target flight operates a Boeing 787 or 777 with JAL's "Sky Suite" business class product. Older aircraft on some routes may have a less desirable cabin configuration. Check SeatGuru or JAL's fleet page.

Log into JAL.com with your confirmation number to select your specific seat and pre-order your meal. JAL offers both Western and Japanese cuisine options in business class, and the Japanese multi-course kaiseki meal is the experience worth choosing.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Plan has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

This creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Plan charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy® Is Your On-Ramp

Alaska Mileage Plan has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most important nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy®.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

The more efficient earning strategy for most ChooseFI members is to apply directly for the Alaska Airlines Visa card, which regularly offers strong welcome bonuses, or to fly Alaska-operated flights. Miles in Alaska Mileage Plan never expire, which means you can accumulate patiently without pressure.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit almost no other major US program offers anymore. On a one-way award from the US to Japan, you could stop in Tokyo for several days, then continue to another destination, all for the same 60,000 miles. This is an advanced move that can double the value of a single award ticket.

Book at up to 331 days in advance — Alaska's booking window. For popular travel dates to Japan, searching early is strongly advised.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm the seats exist. Go to jal.com and use JAL's own award search tool. JAL releases excellent Business Class award inventory to partners — this is one of the best-availability premium cabin routes in the game — but you still want to verify before committing.

Search your target dates in "Award Booking" mode. Look for "J" class availability (Business Class). JAL's 787-9 Sky Suite III product operates on the Seattle–Tokyo Narita route, so filter for that routing specifically. Try flexible dates — a day or two of flexibility can reveal significantly more availability. You can search up to 330+ days out, so don't wait until the last minute.

You need 60,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per one-way Business Class ticket. Check your existing Alaska Mileage Plan balance at alaskaair.com. If you're short, your transfer path is Marriott Bonvoy® at a 3:1 ratio — so 60,000 Alaska miles requires 180,000 Marriott Bonvoy® points (though you'll receive a 5,000-mile bonus when transferring 60,000 Marriott points at a time, so plan accordingly).

Initiate transfers at marriott.com under "Transfer Points." Build in 1 to 5 days for the transfer to post to your Alaska account. Do not call Alaska to book until the miles are confirmed in your balance.

Alaska partner awards with JAL must be booked by phone — you cannot book JAL awards on Alaska's website. Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522. Have the following ready:

Tell the agent you'd like to book a partner award on JAL using miles. Give them the exact flight number and date. Agents are generally familiar with this redemption — it's a popular one.

Before you finalize, confirm the total cost. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on partner awards, so your out-of-pocket should be taxes only. If an agent quotes you a surcharge, politely clarify — this is a known Alaska policy. The total cash component should be well under $200.

If your ideal dates show no availability, try these tactics: search plus or minus three days, look at alternate departure cities (JAL also operates from Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York), or set a calendar reminder to check again — JAL sometimes releases additional inventory closer to departure as business travelers book and cancel. The 331-day booking window means early searchers have the best selection.

Alaska Airlines is not part of any major airline alliance (Star Alliance, Oneworld, or SkyTeam), which gives it unusual freedom to set its own partner award pricing. While alliance members must coordinate pricing frameworks, Alaska negotiates individual deals with each partner airline. This independence is why Alaska can price JAL business class at 60,000 miles when alliance-member programs charge 70,000-100,000 miles for the same seats. The tradeoff is that Alaska's partner award availability can be more limited than what you would find through an alliance booking, making timing and flexibility critical.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner are planning a trip to Japan in the spring — cherry blossom season, the dream itinerary for so many in the ChooseFI community.

The Route: Seattle (SEA) → Tokyo Narita (NRT) on JAL Flight 009, operated by a Boeing 787-9.

The Cash Price: Pull up JAL.com during late March and you'll routinely see Business Class fares at $7,000–$8,500 per person one way. For a couple, that's $14,000–$17,000 in cash for two seats in the premium cabin. Most people stare at that number and close the browser.

The Points Price: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. For two passengers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles plus approximately $200–$250 in taxes. Total cash outlay: roughly $225 for the pair.

The CPP: At a conservative $7,000 cash fare, 60,000 miles delivers 11.7 cents per point — nearly six times the standard benchmark for a great redemption.

JAL's inflight service is consistently ranked among the best in the world. The meal service features both Western and Japanese options, sake and premium spirits, and attentive crew who seem genuinely delighted to serve you. The 9–10 hour flight to Narita passes in quiet, restful comfort. You arrive refreshed.

For a couple targeting FI, spending 120,000 Alaska miles — earned largely through welcome bonuses and everyday spending — instead of $15,000+ in cash is the entire philosophy in action.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days before departure. For cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and Golden Week (late April through early May), JAL Business Class award space is competitive. Set a calendar reminder and search on JAL.com starting at day 335 — then call Alaska the moment the window opens if you see available seats.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — one of the most underused benefits in the program. On a US-to-Japan routing, you could stop in Tokyo for four or five days, then continue to Osaka or another Japanese city (on a separate ticket), effectively getting a multi-city Japan trip from a single 60,000-mile award. Discuss this with the Alaska agent when booking.

Given Alaska's limited transfer partners, the most reliable path to a large Alaska miles balance is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card, which regularly offers welcome bonuses of 40,000–75,000 miles. Stack two cardholders in your household — you and your partner each earn a welcome bonus — and you have a round-trip business class redemption funded almost entirely from sign-up offers.

Marriott-to-Alaska transfers take 1 to 5 days and are irreversible. Never initiate the transfer until you've confirmed the award space exists on JAL.com. Transferring speculatively and then discovering the seat is gone is a painful and costly mistake.

While JAL does release excellent inventory — hence the availability score of 4 out of 5 — "year round" availability doesn't mean unlimited. Japanese holidays (Golden Week, Obon in August, New Year's) see compressed availability. The best open inventory is typically September through November and January through mid-February.

Alaska's policy is no fuel surcharges on partner awards, but always verify the final tax-and-fee total before giving your credit card number. Your total out-of-pocket should be well under $200 per ticket. If it's higher, ask the agent to itemize.

This redemption is built for the ChooseFI couple or solo traveler who has been intentionally accumulating Alaska miles — or Marriott Bonvoy® points — and wants to experience transpacific Business Class without the $8,000 price tag. If Japan is on your bucket list and you're willing to do a phone call to complete the booking, this is one of the highest-value redemptions in the entire loyalty ecosystem.

Minimum points needed: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. A couple needs 120,000 miles for two one-way Business Class tickets.

This redemption is rated **moderate** — and that rating is honest. It's not beginner-friendly (rated 2 out of 5 for beginners), but it's absolutely achievable for anyone willing to learn the two-step process. **What makes it moderate:** First, earning Alaska miles is less straightforward than earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex points. Alaska has **no direct credit card transfer partners** in the major bank ecosystems, which means you can't funnel everyday Amex or Chase spend into Alaska miles directly. You're relying on Alaska co-branded credit cards or the Marriott Bonvoy® transfer path. Second, partner award bookings **cannot be completed online** — you must call Alaska Mileage Plan. For travelers accustomed to booking everything digitally, this feels like friction. In practice, the call takes 15–20 minutes with a prepared agent and is genuinely straightforward. Third, while availability is rated 4 out of 5 (excellent by transpacific standards), you still need to plan ahead, particularly for peak Japan travel seasons. **Three tips to make it easier:** 1. **Start with the Alaska Airlines Visa card** — it's the most direct route to a large Alaska miles balance and regularly offers competitive welcome bonuses. 2. **Do your availability research on JAL.com before calling** — walk into that phone call with the flight number, date, and cabin class already confirmed. The booking becomes a five-minute transaction. 3. **Book 6–10 months out** for peak dates — this eliminates most of the availability stress and gives you time to transfer points if needed. If you've already booked one partner award by phone with any airline, this will feel familiar. If this is your first, the effort is absolutely worth it for a redemption worth 8–17 cents per point.

No. Alaska Mileage Plan is not a transfer partner of Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards. Your primary earning paths are the Alaska Airlines credit card, Marriott Bonvoy® transfers, and purchasing miles during Alaska's periodic sales.

No. JAL flights booked with Alaska miles do not carry fuel surcharges. You will pay only government taxes and fees, typically $25-$50 for a one-way transpacific ticket. This is a major advantage over booking through some other programs.

The best availability appears right at the 331-day booking window. Shoulder seasons like January-February and September-November tend to have more open seats. Cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and summer are the most competitive periods.

Marriott Bonvoy® points transfer to Alaska at a 3:1 ratio. For every 60,000 Bonvoy points transferred, you receive 20,000 Alaska miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus, totaling 25,000 Alaska miles. To reach 60,000 Alaska miles, you would need approximately 135,000 Bonvoy points (factoring in the bonus on each 60K tranche).

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Alaska Mileage Plan to JAL business class is one of the best-kept sweet spots in travel rewards. At 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges, you get access to a world-class cabin at roughly half the mileage cost of competing programs. The earning path is narrower than programs with multiple transfer partners, but for anyone willing to build Alaska miles intentionally, the 8-13 cents per mile value on JAL business class to Japan is extraordinarily difficult to beat.

Choosing a laptop for graphic design work isn't the same as choosing one for surfing and emails. The screen quality, RAM and processing speed are all going to make a difference to your work and how long it takes to power through it. And so while the Black Friday sales have discounts on a dizzying array of laptops, not all of these laptops will measure up to your needs.

To make things easier for you, I've picked out the best laptop deals for graphic designers who split their time between home, studio and clients, and need something both portable and powerful.

Some of these deals are in the UK and some in the US, so we've marked each one accordingly. Here's what's on offer, from the cheapest up.

Intel Core 5 320 | 8GB RAM | 512GB SSD | 14in 1920 x 1200 IPS, 120Hz | 1.19kg

Acer's Swift Air pairs a sage green aluminium body with a smooth 120Hz screen, and at 1.19kg it's easy to carry all day. With 8GB of RAM, it's best for lighter design work such as Figma, Canva and quick photo edits rather than hefty Photoshop files, but it's great value at under $450.

Snapdragon X2 Plus | 16GB RAM | 256GB SSD | 13in 2880 x 1920 touchscreen, 120Hz | keyboard sold separatelyIf you sketch as much as you type, Microsoft's latest 2-in-1 makes a lot of sense. Its 13-inch 120Hz touchscreen works with the Surface Slim Pen, and the kickstand folds back for drawing. Budget extra for the keyboard and pen, though, as neither is included, and check your key apps run on Arm.

Intel Core Ultra X7 358H | Intel Arc B390 graphics | 32GB RAM | 1TB SSD | 16in 2880 x 1800 OLED touchscreen, 120Hz, 100% DCI-P3 | 1.6kg

The most powerful laptop on this list gives you a big 16-inch OLED touchscreen with 100% DCI-P3 coverage, 32GB of RAM and Intel's new Panther Lake chip with Arc B390 graphics, in a body weighing about 1.6kg. That's a serious setup for photo, design and light video editing work.

Intel Core 5 320 | 8GB RAM | 512GB SSD | 14in 1920 x 1200 IPS, 120Hz | 1.19kg

This is the budget pick, but it’s a stylish one, with an aluminium body in sage green and a weight of just 1.19kg. The 8GB of RAM limits you to lighter work such as Figma, Canva and quick photo edits, but for students and side projects it's a lot of laptop for £499.

AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 | RAM: 16-32GB | 1TB SSD | 14in OLED, 100% DCI-P3 | 1.29kg

Step up to this Copilot+ PC and you get an OLED screen covering 100% of the DCI-P3 colour space, which matters if you work with colour. We reviewed the Intel version and found it handles photo editing and web design well, though it struggles with heavy video and 3D work.

Snapdragon X2 Plus | 16GB RAM | 256GB SSD | 13in 2880 x 1920 touchscreen, 120Hz | keyboard sold separatelyAmazon is offering a huge discount on the Microsoft Surface Pro, with a stunning £750 off. This is the top-tier OLED version with the faster 12-core Snapdragon X2 Elite and 1TB of storage. With pen support, it makes a superb digital sketchbook. The keyboard and Slim Pen cost extra, though, and it runs on Arm, so check your apps first.

For most graphic designers, RAM matters more than anything else on the spec sheet. With 8GB, you'll be fine in browser-based tools such as Figma and Canva, but 16GB is a sensible minimum if you spend your days in Photoshop or Illustrator, and 32GB gives you room to grow.

If you work on photography or print, an OLED screen with full DCI-P3 coverage is worth paying extra for. If you like to sketch, the Surface Pro's pen support puts it in a category of its own, as long as the apps you rely on run happily on Arm.

As with all Black Friday deals, these prices may not last long, and stock on the most popular models can sell out quickly. If none of these laptops quite fits your needs, take a look at our guide to the best laptops for graphic design, which we update regularly with our latest recommendations.

#8798. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

Product placement might not be the same under Pattinson's tenure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond and brings with him a host of luxury deals and an audience that’s grown up alongside him. Matt Kerr, Global Executive Creative Director at Marks, shares what he feels brands will need to do to belong in his version of Bond’s world.

Robert Pattinson has only just got the coveted job as the most famous secret agent on earth, and there’s already speculation around who’ll cut his first dinner jacket. Craig wore Tom Ford, but Pattinson has enjoyed a longstanding relationship with Dior. I’m interested in who gets the job, of course – but I’d like to see what Pattinson does in the suit first.

There’s a little bit of danger in Pattinson’s acting. He has this laid-back British cool thing going on, but there’s also a bit of an awkward edge to him – he’s a bit of a conundrum, and I’d s say there’s something of Fleming’s Bond in that. So, for an agency taking a brief or a brand handing one out, I’d start there. What would this particular Bond choose, and when would we get to see why he chose it?

Fleming was deliberate in showcasing what Bond would buy – he understood his protagonist and the pleasure his audience would get from finding out. The Sea Island cotton shirt, the Rolex, the Aston Martin. You could read the books as a shopping list for a certain idea of British masculinity. The list was interesting because it belonged to a man who had his reasons for choosing things.

Take the silver Aston Martin in Goldfinger. An iconic scene is Bond flipping open the top of the gearstick and sending his passenger through the roof. I couldn’t tell you how long the badge was in shot. But the car still got the punchline. Yes, you can hand over some serious investment to get your car brand into a Bond film, but it’s the association with the scene and the interaction with the hero that people buy into.

I’d give a watch brand the same brief. For No Time to Die, Omega developed the Seamaster Diver 300M 007 Edition with input from Daniel Craig and the filmmakers, then put it on sale to the public. Craig wanted a lightweight watch that felt right for a military man, so Omega made it in titanium. That’s where I’d start with Pattinson too. Work out what his Bond would choose and why. If the audience can see why he’d wear it, they’ve got a reason to want one for themselves.

Brands also need to think about the audience. Yes, Bond is the ultimate masculine icon, but Pattinson is an icon to women in their thirties because they grew up with him. For the teen girl who saw the first Twilight movie at 15, Pattinson is her pin-up. And if he stays with the franchise for the best part of a decade – which seems to be the norm – that young girl will be in her forties. So, I’d have that in mind when I was briefing the campaign.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Take a hotel partnership. There’s a familiar version of that ad where a man books a weekend so he can spend it feeling like Bond. According to Nielsen data, women influence 70 to 80% of consumer spending, so maybe brands should ask what a hotel brand could offer a woman who has followed Pattinson for years and fancies booking the weekend herself. Give her a detail to spot at check-in and let it pay off later that evening. She gets to have some of the fun Bond has in the film. If the partnership carries through to another film, the hotel can give her something different to come back for.

I’d keep the gun barrel iconography and every word of the slick one-liner, “Bond, James Bond”, but I’d give Pattinson room to play with the pause. We know the line so well that we’ll hear the difference. And I’d make this the rule for every brand partner. Make it make sense for Bond but show me what makes it right for Pattinson’s Bond.

When the first design concepts come in, I’d put my thumb over the 007 mark. If the cufflink shot underneath could sell any Saville Row suit, I’d send the team back to the drawing board. It must fit this new era of Bond - something that Craig’s or Connery’s might have passed on.

Some of the old partnerships will still fit. Others will need to go or evolve with the way he plays Bond and the audience that will spend the next decade watching him. For a brand planning its next five to ten years, the next Bond film might be the last great monoculture event.

Matt Kerr is a Global Executive Creative Director at Marks with more than 20 years’ experience shaping brands and leading creative teams. His work spans brand identity, packaging, campaigns and digital experiences for clients including LEGO, Diageo, Reckitt and Haleon. At Marks, he has helped transform the agency’s strategic design offering and leads creative standards across a global community of more than 500 designers.
