#8768. designboom’s guide to miami art week 2026: what to see in and out of the fairs

explore must-see highlights of art basel miami beach, design miami, and other standout shows and events across the city.

Miami Art Week returns from November 30th to December 6th, 2026, bringing a packed program of art fairs, outdoor installations, exhibitions, and unexpected encounters across Miami and Miami Beach. This year, the city becomes a setting for everything from giant mirrored disco balls and interactive robots to surreal theatrical environments and public sculptures built for play.

Art Basel Miami Beach returns with a reconfigured fair and an expanded digital art program, while Design Miami explores the stories behind collectible objects through its curatorial theme, Unveiling. Beyond the convention center, the Miami Design District welcomes a series of interactive sculptural installations by Objects of Common Interest, and Faena Beach becomes a dance floor beneath a monumental mirrored sphere by Christopher Joshua Benton.

Meanwhile, CJ Hendry invites visitors into a swimming-pool-sized pit of oversized pills, Marcel Dzama brings his dreamlike universe to Lincoln Road, and Miami’s galleries and museums open new exhibitions. From established fairs to temporary interventions along the beachfront, here’s designboom’s guide to what to see across Miami Art Week 2026.

Art Basel Miami Beach returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with 272 exhibitors from more than 40 countries and territories. For 2026, the fair introduces a reconfigured floor plan with a smaller overall footprint, longer sightlines, and established international galleries distributed throughout the space alongside younger exhibitors.

The fair’s main sectors bring together contemporary work and historic presentations, with Nova focusing on recently created pieces, Positions supporting emerging artists through solo booths, and Survey revisiting overlooked artistic practices. More than 30 galleries will participate for the first time, with a strong presence from Latin America and the Caribbean.

Zero 10, Art Basel’s platform dedicated to art of the digital era, returns with Generation, an exhibition curated by Karen Archey and Eli Scheinman. Featuring 19 projects, the presentation explores how digital technology is changing the ways art is made and experienced, with works by artists including Refik Anadol and Sarah Meyohas.

what: Art Basel Miami Beach when: December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2–3) where: Miami Beach Convention Center, 1901 Convention Center Drive, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Design Miami returns for its 22nd edition with more than 75 exhibitors bringing together historic and contemporary collectible design. Under the direction of curator Charlene Prempeh, the 2026 fair follows the theme Unveiling, inviting visitors to look more closely at the cultural histories and making processes behind the objects on display.

The program spans established galleries and emerging practices, with furniture, lighting, and sculptural works presented alongside experimental installations. The fair’s Curio section provides a platform for more focused design presentations, while special projects and collaborations extend the program beyond the traditional gallery booth.

As one of the main events of Miami Art Week, Design Miami brings together designers, collectors, and galleries working across different generations of material experimentation and craftsmanship.

what: Design Miami when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 (invitation-only previews December 1st and 2nd) where: Convention Center Drive and 19th Street, Miami Beach, FL

Untitled Art celebrates its 15th Miami Beach edition with more than 170 galleries and nonprofit organizations representing 36 countries and territories. The fair returns to its beachfront pavilion along Ocean Drive, offering a curated selection of contemporary art with an emphasis on emerging practices and independent galleries.

The 2026 edition features five sectors: Main, Artist Spotlight, Nest, Non-Profit, and Special Projects. Artist Spotlight, curated by Agustina Ferreyra, brings together focused solo presentations, while Nest, curated by Willem Molesworth, explores collaboration and exchange across East Asia and the wider international art scene.

With 53 first-time exhibitors joining the program, the fair continues to create space for younger galleries alongside established international participants.

what: Untitled Art when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: Ocean Drive and 12th Street, Miami Beach, FL

The New Art Dealers Alliance returns to Ice Palace Studios for the 24th edition of NADA Miami, bringing together 135 exhibitors from 63 cities and 27 countries.

Known for its focus on independent galleries and emerging artistic practices, NADA presents work from both established and younger art spaces. Its relatively informal setting offers an opportunity to discover artists working across painting, installation, sculpture, and experimental media, with presentations that often take a more exploratory approach than those found at the larger international fairs.

The event occupies Ice Palace Studios in downtown Miami, with exhibitions and programming extending into its outdoor areas.

what: NADA when: December 1st — 5th, 2026 where: Ice Palace Studios, 1400 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33136

Art Miami returns to its waterfront pavilion at One Herald Plaza with an international selection of modern and contemporary art. One of Miami’s longest-running art fairs, the event brings together established galleries presenting works from the 20th and 21st centuries.

The fair spans painting, sculpture, photography, and installation, with a program that moves between historically significant artists and contemporary practices. Alongside conventional gallery presentations, visitors can expect individual artist projects and interactive installations, including a new felt environment by British artist Lucy Sparrow.

Located in downtown Miami, the fair takes place alongside its sister event CONTEXT Art Miami, allowing visitors to move between the two exhibitions.

what: Art Miami when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: One Herald Plaza, NE 14th Street, Miami, FL 33132

Running alongside Art Miami, CONTEXT Art Miami returns to One Herald Plaza with a focus on emerging and mid-career contemporary artists. The sister fair brings together 75 international galleries presenting new work and curated solo exhibitions.

Established in 2012, CONTEXT offers a platform for galleries working with younger artists and those developing new approaches to familiar media. The fair also features installations and projects created specifically for the event, offering visitors a view of contemporary practices beyond the more established market represented at Art Miami.

what: CONTEXT Art Miami when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: CONTEXT Art Miami Pavilion, One Herald Plaza, NE 14th Street, Miami, FL 33132

Amsterdam-based Studio DRIFT brings Murmuring Minds to Art Basel Miami Beach’s Zero 10 sector, presented with the digital art platform TAEX. The installation transforms an arena of autonomous robotic blocks into a responsive environment, with their movement shifting according to the actions of visitors.

Entering the space, one person at a time can influence the robots as they move collectively, follow a lead, or behave according to patterns inspired by wind and natural swarms. The project draws on DRIFT’s long-running research into collective behavior, particularly the coordinated movements of birds and other living systems.

The presentation also includes Coded Nature, an interactive digital series in which algorithmically generated swarms respond to visitors’ gestures. Together, the works examine how individual actions influence the behavior of larger systems.

what: Studio DRIFT, Murmuring Minds and Coded Nature when: December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2–3) where: Art Basel Miami Beach, Zero 10, Miami Beach Convention Center

At Art Basel’s Zero 10, Sarah Meyohas presents Phase Transition, a new installation of organic, sculptural forms that appear to communicate through movement and sound. Presented by Boesky Gallery, the work brings together magnetized liquid, algorithmic systems, and synthesizers to create a strange conversation among objects.

The forms rest on mesh pedestals or hang from suspended wires. Cutout windows reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing magnetic particles that shift in response to programmed magnets. These movements are translated into sound, allowing each sculpture to participate in an ongoing exchange.

Their rounded, bodily shapes reference biological growth and transformation, while their mechanical conversations raise questions about intelligence and communication beyond human language. The installation extends Meyohas’ interest in the relationship between organic life and emerging technologies.

what: Sarah Meyohas: Phase Transition when: December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2nd — 3rd) where: Art Basel Miami Beach, Zero 10, Miami Beach Convention Center

During Miami Art Week this December, artist Derrick Adams and the LEGO Group will bring a nine-foot unicorn pool float to Miami Beach. Built from LEGO bricks, the oversized figure will sit at the center of Pool Party, a colorful installation at Avant Gallery inside 1111 Lincoln Road. The project takes Adams’ long-running Floaters series, with its images of Black people at leisure, into an entirely different medium.

On December 3rd and 4th, visitors will have a hand in creating the artwork themselves. Adams and the LEGO team will invite the public to help assemble parts of the installation, ahead of its completed unveiling on December 5th. The two-day community build is part of The Art of Building, a participatory experience organized during Miami Art Week — RSVP here!

what: Derrick Adams x LEGO: The Art of Building when: December 3rd — 4th, 2026 (completed installation reveal December 5th) where: Avant Gallery, 1111 Lincoln Road, Miami Beach, Florida

Japanese artist Tadashi Kawamata brings a site-specific installation to Collins Park in collaboration with Maison Ruinart during Art Basel Miami Beach. Part of the champagne house’s ongoing Conversations with Nature program, the work draws on Kawamata’s observations of Ruinart’s historic vineyards in France.

Known for his temporary architectural constructions made from lightweight materials, Kawamata approaches installation as a process of responding to a place. His Miami commission continues that interest through a large-scale structure that invites visitors to reconsider their relationship with the surrounding environment.

what: Tadashi Kawamata x Maison Ruinart when: December 3rd — 6th, 2026 where: Collins Park, Miami Beach, FL

Dutch designer Iris van Herpen brings her collaboration with Maison Perrier-Jouët to Design Miami, following its presentation in Tokyo and Paris earlier this year. The project grew from her selection as the inaugural recipient of the Perrier-Jouët Design for Nature Award.

Drawing on cymatics, the study of how vibrations produce visible patterns, van Herpen translated signals associated with the living ecosystem of the champagne house’s vineyards into sculptural forms.

The resulting creations include Symphonic Bloom, a one-of-a-kind artwork made from recycled golden metal and silk surrounding a historic champagne bottle, and Symphonic Life, a limited series of sculptural sleeves adorned with gold. The pieces carry van Herpen’s interest in natural structures into the scale of collectible objects.

what: Iris van Herpen x Maison Perrier-Jouët when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: Design Miami, Convention Center Drive and 19th Street, Miami Beach

British artist Lucy Sparrow returns to Art Miami with The Money Laundry, an interactive installation that transforms a familiar laundromat into a shop filled with handmade felt objects.

Among the colorful boxes of detergent and cleaning supplies, visitors will find painted felt banknotes, imitation luxury watches, and passports created by the artist. Sparrow will also exchange $100 in real money for a bundle of felt currency carrying a fictional value of $600.

An on-site photo booth allows guests to have their own felt passports painted live, extending the artist’s ongoing interest in consumer culture and the objects through which people assign value.

what: Lucy Sparrow: The Money Laundry when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: Art Miami, Booth AM207, One Herald Plaza, Miami

Artist Christopher Joshua Benton transforms Faena Beach into a temporary dance floor with A Lore Supreme, a monumental kinetic sculpture that reimagines the disco ball as a map of Miami’s cultural history.

The mirrored sphere rises 27 feet above the sand and stretches 44 feet across. Its surface is composed of around 7,000 reflective facets, which move with the wind and scatter images of the surrounding beach.

Partially embedded in the ground, the sculpture becomes both a gathering place and a setting for music and performance.

Drawing on research into Miami’s musical communities, Benton incorporates recorded conversations and sound from local DJs and musicians. The installation traces the influence of African, Caribbean, and Latin American cultures on the city’s music, turning the beach into an open-air space for listening and dancing.

what: Christopher Joshua Benton: A Lore Supreme when: December 1st — 6th, 2026, noon-9 p.m. where: Faena Beach, 3201 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

The Miami Design District’s 11th Annual Design Commission has been awarded to Objects of Common Interest, the New York- and Athens-based studio founded by Eleni Petaloti and Leonidas Trampoukis.

Titled Out of This World: A Field of Conditions, the installation places six abstract sculptures throughout the neighborhood. Some release clouds of vapor into the Miami air, while others rotate when touched or distort their surroundings through reflective surfaces. A marble-and-resin pyramid produces sound that becomes audible only when visitors approach.

Developed through the studio’s ongoing experiments with resin, marble, and movement, the commission extends into Design Miami with a companion installation, Out of This World: A Certain Attraction. There, a concealed sculptural object responds to the presence of visitors, shifting to reveal fragmented reflections of those who enter.

what: Objects of Common Interest, Out of This World: A Field of Conditions when: during Miami Art Week 2026 (exact opening date to be confirmed) where: various locations throughout the Miami Design District, Miami, FL

Artist Marcel Dzama brings his distinctive universe of masked figures and theatrical imagery to Miami Beach with Who Loves the Moon?, an immersive installation presented by Capital One and The Cultivist.

The experience begins with a giant Moon that opens its mouth to welcome visitors inside. From there, guests move through a series of environments incorporating illuminated optical works, puppetry, and imagery drawn from Dzama’s paintings and films.

The journey culminates in a theatrical landscape with checkerboard floors and towering palms. By day, visitors can play chess and explore tarot and astrological readings. Evening programming introduces music and performances by Miami City Ballet, bringing the artist’s imagined world into motion.

what: Marcel Dzama: Who Loves the Moon? when: December 1st — 4th, 2026 (free public viewing December 3rd — 4th) where: 434 Lincoln Road, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Australian artist CJ Hendry joins Salon 94 Design to bring PASTEL to the Miami Design District, transforming thousands of oversized pills into an immersive landscape of color.

The installation revisits Hendry’s earlier bead-filled environment, this time replacing the familiar spherical forms with sculptural vitamins, supplements, and prescription pills. Visitors can enter the swimming-pool-sized pit, sift through the colorful objects, and assemble their own playful prescriptions.

Through the oversized forms, Hendry turns familiar products associated with health and self-optimization into objects for interaction and play.

what: CJ Hendry x Salon 94 Design: PASTEL Miami when: November 30th — December 20th, 2026 where: 3925 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33127

At The Ritz-Carlton, South Beach, American artist Rachel Lee Hovnanian presents The Perfect Trade-Off, a solo exhibition exploring how technology has changed the ways people spend time together.

In the hotel’s Art Deco lobby, Dinner for Ten stages an elaborate meal with ten places at the table. Nine chairs are occupied by monitors depicting individuals absorbed in their phones, leaving a single empty seat for visitors. As the feast deteriorates, the work considers what happens to shared rituals when attention turns toward digital devices.

The exhibition extends onto the beachfront with Poor Teddy in Memoriam, a monumental bronze teddy bear surrounded by flowers. Elsewhere, a vintage three-wheeled Piaggio Ape has been transformed into a functioning phone-charging station, bringing Hovnanian’s examination of our relationship with technology into a familiar, everyday encounter.

what: Rachel Lee Hovnanian: The Perfect Trade-Off when: December 1st — 8th, 2026 where: The Ritz-Carlton, South Beach, 1 Lincoln Road, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Argentine artist and designer Andrés Reisinger brings his dreamlike architectural imagery into physical space with Do You Dream In Color?, a property-wide exhibition at Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa.

Known for his surreal digital environments and all-pink architectural takeovers, Reisinger will transform parts of the hotel through immersive installations and digital artworks. At the entrance, one of his signature draped interventions will cover the architecture in flowing fabric-like forms, while more digital works appear throughout Bar Centro and the hotel’s screens.

The exhibition is presented with ArtRepublic, and brings Reisinger’s digitally conceived aesthetic into an environment that visitors can experience in-person.

what: Andrés Reisinger: Do You Dream In Color? when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa, 4041 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

Greek designer Natalia Triantafylli presents Under the Libra Sun at Villa Paula in Miami’s Little Haiti neighborhood, marking her first major exhibition and largest-scale work to date. Presented by The Future Perfect, the collection takes inspiration from the historic villa’s original tiles and gardens, with pieces that reinterpret Greek and Victorian ornament through bright colors and floral patterns.

Triantafylli hand-sculpts forms in clay before scanning them and combining them with 3D-printed counterparts. The collection includes two monumental porcelain chandeliers, decorative mirrors, column-capital tables and stools, and her first upholstered pieces. Several works are developed with her partner, artist Andrew Pierce Scott, whose blackened steel structures contrast with her richly patterned ceramics. The pieces are bolted together rather than glued to leave their construction visible.

what: Natalia Triantafylli: Under the Libra Sun, presented by The Future Perfect when: opening November 30th, 2026 where: Villa Paula, 5811 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33127

Bosnian artist Radenko Milak presents Algorithms for the Future at Piero Atchugarry Gallery in Miami, his first solo exhibition in the city. Curated by Claire Breukel, the show brings together hyperrealistic black-and-white watercolors that examine how technology shapes our memories of the past and visions of the future. Drawing from archival photography, science fiction, and architecture, Milak combines familiar imagery with imagined scenarios, from Edward Hopper’s solitary figures to futuristic skyscrapers filled with surveillance equipment.

Among the works is White Noise (2026), which merges a warped urban tower with vintage recording devices, and Ghost Game, a series of 23 paintings tracing the history of artificial intelligence through mathematics, cinema, and popular culture. Each image is painted by hand with near-photographic precision, a deliberately slow process that contrasts with the speed of algorithmically generated pictures. The works question what happens when machines begin to determine how history is represented and remembered.

what: Radenko Milak: Algorithms for the Future, curated by Claire Breukel when: November 29th, 2026 — April 18, 2027 where: Piero Atchugarry Gallery, 5520 NE 4th Avenue, Miami, FL 33137

Design Hotels teams up with Play-Doh for Designed to Play, a five-day program at The Shelborne by Proper in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2026. At its center is an installation by Copenhagen-based Helle Mardahl Studio, created in collaboration with Hasbro’s new Blooms by Play-Doh collection. The project marks an unusual moment for the familiar modeling compound, which has introduced its first line developed specifically for adults in the brand’s 70-year history.

Throughout the week, visitors can experiment with the colorful material in hands-on workshops and create their own sculptural bouquets. The hotel will also host morning conversations on creativity and design, while New York’s Pawn Chess Club brings custom chessboards and open games to the space. The program takes a playful approach to the usual Miami Art Week schedule, with opportunities to make something, try a new game, or simply spend an afternoon experimenting.

what: Design Hotels x Play-Doh, Designed to Play, featuring Helle Mardahl Studio when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: The Shelborne by Proper, 1801 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Miami’s Wynwood Arts District welcomes Grotto Baths on December 1, a 7,500-square-foot social bathhouse that brings contemporary art into the centuries-old tradition of communal bathing. Designed by Antoinette Marie Johnson in collaboration with Stokes Architecture + Design, the interiors draw from Brazilian modernism, with curved archways, geometric tile patterns, and bursts of orange and blue against natural stone and travertine. Visitors move between thermal pools and cold plunges, while a 30-person cedar sauna hosts guided rituals accompanied by aromatic steam.

Art plays a central role in the new space. Miami-based artist Emmett Moore has created site-specific sculptures and custom benches using reclaimed materials inspired by South Florida’s limestone and mid-century breeze-block architecture. Works by Papou appear in the lobby, and an exterior mural by Mandy Ann takes inspiration from water. The phone-free bathhouse also includes a garden café, with special food and drinks inspired by Moore’s installations planned for Miami Art Week.

what: Grotto Baths, featuring site-specific installations by Emmett Moore when: Opens December 1st, 2026, for members (day-pass access begins December 7th) where: Grotto Baths, 325 NW 28th Street, Miami, FL 33127

At Nobu Hotel Miami Beach, Japanese artist and ceramic conservator Naoko Fukumaru presents a collection of works exploring the centuries-old practice of kintsugi, the repair of broken ceramics using lacquer and gold.

Presented in collaboration with The Morikami Museum and Japanese Gardens, the lobby exhibition brings together ceramic objects that have been broken, discarded, or altered through firing. Fukumaru reconstructs their forms using natural urushi lacquer and 23.5-karat gold, leaving visible lines that trace the histories of the objects.

With more than three decades of experience in ceramic conservation, the Kyoto-born artist approaches repair as an opportunity to give damaged objects a new visual identity.

what: Naoko Fukumaru: The Kintsugi Art of Naoko Fukumaru when: November 25th — December 7th, 2026 where: Nobu Hotel Miami Beach, 4525 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

Miami’s Little River neighborhood welcomes a new cultural space with the opening of Mitrani Art, a multidisciplinary center dedicated to photography, video art, and film.

Founded by sisters Dina and Rhonda Mitrani and designed by R&R Studios, the project transforms a former mechanic shop into galleries and artist studios, with a screening room and outdoor courtyard. The opening marks a new chapter for the sisters, who previously operated the Mitrani Warehouse in Wynwood.

The inaugural exhibition, ReExposures: The Magic Within, brings together artists who have contributed to their programs over the years. Works range from large-scale photographic experiments to video installations, including a monumental photogram by Roberto Huarcaya and Antonia Wright’s video Suddenly We Jumped, in which the artist breaks through panes of glass.

what: Mitrani Art, ReExposures: The Magic Within when: Opening November 30th, 2026 (6-9 p.m. reception) where: Mitrani Art, 7325 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33150

The Bass in Miami Beach presents a season of exhibitions that bring visitors into direct contact with the works on view, from interactive environments to sculptural installations.

In the museum’s Rotunda, Argentine artist Amalia Pica presents Lecturas Posibles, an almost two-dimensional library where surfaces become chalkboards. Visitors are invited to write and draw across the installation, creating an evolving collection of marks and messages.

Elsewhere, Japanese artist Yuko Mohri’s Unviolated Imperfection explores everyday objects through unpredictable mechanical systems, while architecture and design duo Pedro y Juana transform an interior with patterned surfaces and custom furniture for Aquí. Their richly colored environment draws on Miami’s subtropical setting, inviting visitors to spend time within the installation.

what: The Bass 2026-2027 exhibition season, featuring Amalia Pica, Yuko Mohri, and Pedro y Juana when: exhibitions on view throughout Miami Art Week 2026 where: Bass Museum of Art, 2100 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33139

LVMH The Studio Miami returns for its sixth edition, bringing a five-day program of contemporary art and creative workshops to the Miami Design District.

The pop-up gallery presents works by ten artists working across painting, sculpture, textiles, photography, and digital media. Participating artists include Cavier Coleman, Glenneisha Darkins, Jay Chung, and Kristen White, alongside others exploring identity and cultural history through different materials.

Alongside the exhibition, visitors can attend public conversations and craftsmanship demonstrations organized with artisans and creative partners from Louis Vuitton, Tiffany & Co., and TAG Heuer.

what: LVMH The Studio Miami 2026 when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026, 11 a.m.-4 p.m. where: Palm Court Event Space, 140 NE 39th Street, 3rd Floor, Miami, FL 33137

The Craig Robins Collection unveils its 2026-2027 rehang, Real Shadows, featuring more than 300 works of modern and contemporary art and design.

Presented at Dacra’s headquarters in the Miami Design District, the exhibition brings together pieces by John Baldessari, Charles Ray, and Marlene Dumas, alongside recent acquisitions by artists including Alex Da Corte and Lauren Halsey.

Taking its title from Baldessari’s Tetrad Series (1999), the exhibition explores the persistence of images through painting and sculpture. The presentation also incorporates significant design objects by Zaha Hadid, Jean Prouvé, and Ron Arad, reflecting the collection’s long-standing relationship between art and furniture.

what: Craig Robins Collection: Real Shadows when: 2026-2027; Wednesdays-Fridays, noon-4 p.m., by appointment where: Dacra Headquarters, 3841 NE 2nd Avenue, Miami, FL 33137

El Espacio 23 in Miami’s Allapattah neighborhood presents Nothing Is Linear: Relations Across Latin America and Its Diasporas, a new exhibition drawn from the Jorge M. Pérez Collection. Bringing together more than 130 works by 120 artists, the exhibition examines the region’s shifting cultural identities through migration and shared histories. Curated through a collaboration between Anelys Alvarez, Patricia Hanna, Taiyana Pimentel, and Patrick Charpenel, the presentation moves between figurative art, political expression, and abstraction.

Among the works is José Carlos Martinat’s kinetic sculpture Manifestos, whose moving pendulums and speakers broadcast historical art manifestos in their original languages. Elsewhere, Hernan Bas revisits Miami’s brief snowfall in 1977, while works by Julio Le Parc and Adrián Villar Rojas explore different approaches to visual language. Across four interconnected sections, the exhibition considers Latin America as a network of relationships that extends far beyond geographical borders.

what: Nothing Is Linear: Relations Across Latin America and Its Diasporas when: November 19th, 2026 — August 14th, 2027 where: El Espacio 23, 2270 NW 23rd Street, Miami, FL 33142

Jeffrey Deitch presents Ensalada Mixta, an exhibition of work by Swiss artist Urs Fischer in the Miami Design District.

The presentation explores Fischer’s approach to transforming familiar objects through unexpected materials and changes in scale. Working across sculpture and design, the artist draws on industrial processes and common domestic forms, using materials including steel, epoxy, and electrical components.

The exhibition continues Fischer’s long-running interest in the relationship between art objects and the everyday things that surround them, bringing his playful visual language into a temporary gallery setting during Miami Art Week.

what: Urs Fischer: Ensalada Mixta, presented by Jeffrey Deitch when: November 30th — December 23rd, 2026 where: 45 NE 39th Street, Miami, FL 33137

At the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, Basquiat. A Hidden World offers a new perspective on Jean-Michel Basquiat’s paintings through his little-known use of ultraviolet-reactive materials.

Curated by Dieter Buchhart and Anna Karina Hofbauer, the exhibition brings together four works, including Untitled (Orange Sports Figure) (1982), Emblem (1984), Cash Crop (1984), and O.M.R.A.V.S. (1984).

Under ultraviolet light, words and markings hidden within the surfaces become visible. In Emblem, the repeated phrase ‘invisible men’ appears beneath the familiar composition, revealing an additional layer of Basquiat’s visual language.

what: Basquiat: A Hidden World when: November 29th, 2026 — February 12th, 2027 where: ICA Miami Expansion Space, 23 NE 41st Street, Miami, FL 33137

Indian artist Subodh Kerkar brings The Ocean Odyssey to Miami Beach as a free public performance presented by REEFLINE in collaboration with Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa.

The site-specific project brings together more than 50 community participants and dancers from Miami City Ballet, with choreography developed in collaboration with Durante Verzola.

Taking place directly on the beachfront, the performance uses movement to explore the relationship between people and marine environments. The ocean becomes the setting for a temporary gathering that connects contemporary art with Miami’s coastal landscape.

what: Subodh Kerkar: The Ocean Odyssey, presented by REEFLINE when: December 1st, 2026, 4:30-6 p.m. where: Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa beachfront, 4041 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

#8767. Bumps Inside Nose: Common Causes and Top Treatments

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

There are many possible causes for bumps inside your nose — some as harmless as a pimple, others that might need more attention. It’s easy to imagine the worst, but the truth is usually less alarming.

If you’ve got a painful, annoying, or strange bump in your nose, keep reading to learn what it might be, whether it’s worth worrying about, and how to deal with it.

So, what’s behind these bothersome nose bumps? Here are some common culprits:

This is inflammation of the nasal vestibule, the area just inside your nostrils, often caused by bacterial infections. It can lead to painful, red bumps sensitive to the touch. Common triggers include frequent nose-picking, blowing too hard, or even plucking nose hairs.

Like on your face, the pores inside your nose can become clogged with oil, dirt, and bacteria, leading to pimples. These can be painful and may swell, especially in such a sensitive area.

Non-cancerous growths can develop in the nasal passages or sinus lining due to chronic inflammation, allergies, or infections. While they’re usually painless, larger polyps can cause blockages, leading to breathing difficulties, a reduced sense of smell, or recurrent sinus infections.

When you pluck or trim nose hairs, the hair can sometimes grow back into the skin instead of out, causing an ingrown hair. If this becomes infected, it can result in a painful bump inside the nose.

A bump can also form inside the nose due to trauma, such as a blow to the nose, or even from something as simple as aggressive nose-picking. The trauma can cause the tissue to swell or become bruised. In some cases, a hard bump may form as the tissue heals.

Fluid-filled sacs that can form in your nose, usually harmless but sometimes uncomfortable.

A hard bump inside the nose might be due to problems with the cartilage, such as a deviated septum or cartilage overgrowth.

Small, benign bumps that may appear on or in the nose are often mistaken for pimples but are fibrous tissue growths.

Ready to say goodbye to that pesky bump inside your nose? The proper treatment depends on what’s causing it, but here are some ideas to ease the discomfort and promote healing:

Additionally, if you’re dealing with nasal polyps, a healthcare professional might prescribe steroid sprays to shrink them and reduce inflammation, making breathing easier.

On the other hand, if a bacterial infection is the culprit, as in cases of nasal vestibulitis, your doc may recommend a topical antibiotic like mupirocin. This ointment is applied directly inside the nose to target the infection, reduce redness, and promote healing.

While most nose bumps aren’t a big deal, some need more attention. Here’s when to make that appointment:

Even the slightest bump inside your nose can be a major annoyance. Causes vary from harmless pimples to things that require more attention, like polyps.

Self-care measures can usually ease discomfort and speed healing, but if it’s super painful or worrying discharge, it’s time to sniff out professional help.

#8766. Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

Barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—big and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not new, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

For some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

“It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” says Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting new collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is quickly becoming the preferred method.

“[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” says Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

This type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” says Dr. Pearl.

Dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

Try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

For cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

But will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” says Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

If you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

If injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a plan to minimize your pain.

#8765. Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.

Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.

Vinyl lines the inner curves, where Nahleh and Saloojee designed creature-like constellations based on man-made military objects in the sky.

The trio of installations were displayed at three venues at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial – the Al Qasimiyah School, a former slaughterhouse, and in the sandy Al Madam town.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” Nahleh told Dezeen. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

“The drones, missiles, rockets and satellites eclipse some of the constellations, and sometimes fuse with them,” he continued.

“That fusion is at the heart of this project – how do these technologies, through cultural practices on the ground, begin to morph into new creatures and new constellations that people try to make sense of to interpret the violence of this military technology that is taking place.”

Nahleh and Saloojee aimed to combine the reality of modern war with mythical storytelling, drawing upon their research into communities exposed to military attacks.

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures – creatures that fuse together technological advancement with epistemic practices and myth-making practices that happen from the ground,” said Nahleh.

“Most of these creatures, these modern constellations as we’re calling them, are populating the night sky in our drawing alongside pathways of flights of drones, satellites and other things that manifest across the night sky we’ve inherited, rather than the one we lost,” he continued.

“We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us, be it in the shape of missiles, phosphorus, or flares.”

As well as depicting creature-like constellations in their inner curves, the structures themselves were designed as creatures – the nocturnal Solifugi spider known to run out the sun and into shade.

“The project is dedicated to the Solifugi, which is a spider that by nature runs away from the sun, the sun of imperial savagery,” said Nahleh. “It has a very thick skin to protect it from this brightness, and in its belly is a map of the contemporary sky.”

Three openings puncture the shell in each of the installations. In the desert site at Al Madam, a vertical cut-out frames a view of the minaret of a distant mosque, and at the slaughterhouse site, a long opening was set at the height of a cow.

Traditional Hakawati storytellers will narrate stories at the installations as part of the triennial, which runs until April.

“The story is difficult, but it’s about finding optimism,” said Nahleh. “People are carving their own histories on the weapons that are here to annihilate them.”

“There’s a paradox here that we have to confront,” he continued. “When libraries are being erased, and people have no more books to publish or things to write on, they’re writing on the weapons that are sent to devour them.”

“Kids now are finding ways again to dream by placing their wishes upon the shooting stars, which are usually missiles and rockets. It’s a sad and complicated story, but we can no longer escape it by wishing for a sky we no longer have.”

We rounded up eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which includes a draping shelter that pays homage to the improvised learning spaces created by Virginia’s Black community, and a circular canopy with cut-outs that plot 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun.

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#8764. What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

With the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one issue keeps coming up: the side effects. As important as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she says. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”

Fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen says.

You can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen says. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

Fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing issue worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen says: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

Now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation issue), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen says.

With that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen says. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

People who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we said above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen says. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”

Another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

Whatever new fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu says. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

#8763. Mondaine turns solar technology into design feature with Doppio Solar Skeleton timepiece

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton.

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch’s technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the “clarity and legibility” that define the collection.

Powered by a Swiss Ronda solar movement, the watch converts natural and artificial light into electrical energy, which is stored in a rechargeable battery.

According to Mondaine, a few minutes of sunlight can reactivate a fully discharged movement, while a full charge provides a power reserve of up to eight months in complete darkness.

The brand explained that this technology eliminates the need for regular battery replacements, offering a more resource-conscious approach to timekeeping.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton is available in two versions, each offering a different interpretation of its distinctive design.

The first combines a polished silver 316L stainless steel case with a vegan grape leather strap, bringing together traditional watchmaking materials and a contemporary material alternative.

The second features a polished black stainless steel case paired with a matching mesh bracelet, creating a more monochromatic appearance that emphasises the watch’s clean lines and geometric detailing.

Both versions feature a 41-millimetre case, a discreet date window and a precisely laser-etched Mondaine logo and solar markings.

A double-domed sapphire crystal and water resistance of up to 5 ATM complete the design, “combining refined aesthetics with everyday practicality”.

“With the Doppio Solar Skeleton, we wanted to make solar technology part of the design itself,” said Mondaine.

“By revealing the cells beneath the dial, we have created a watch where functionality becomes a defining aesthetic feature, while staying true to Mondaine’s principles of clarity, precision and Swiss design.”

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine’s commitment to iconic Swiss minimalist design, where form and function work together.

By integrating visible solar technology into the collection’s established design language, the watch intends to demonstrate how a functional element can become an integral part of a timepiece’s aesthetic identity.

To find out more about Mondaine and the Doppio Solar Skeleton, visit the brand’s website.

#8762. Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a new reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

The appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”

That role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”

But is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a big deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson says. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial issues that occur with age, Dr. Molina says. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”

As with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson says. It’s also extra important to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

There’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she says—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

#8761. Vegetarian Bodybuilding: 4 Tips to Build Muscle

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

First off, let’s clear up a myth: vegetarian bodybuilders are real! You don’t need chicken breasts or salmon to get ripped. Many vegetarian and vegan bodybuilders have shown you can build muscle and lean without meat.

It might be a bit trickier, but you can achieve great results with the proper planning and knowledge. So, get ready to learn how to master vegetarian bodybuilding!

Building muscle on a vegetarian diet isn’t rocket science, but it requires some know-how. Here are some tips to keep you on track.

Let’s face it: protein is the MVP for muscle building and is even more critical when you’re vegetarian. Aim for around 1.6 – 2.2 g/kg/day. In other words, aim for 0.73 to 1 gram per pound of body weight per day. For example, if you weigh 150 pounds, this would mean you should consume about 110 to 150 grams of protein each day.

If that seems like a lot, don’t fret — there’s a smorgasbord of plant-based proteins to fuel your workouts and keep those muscles fed.

And hey, don’t forget about dairy and eggs if you’re a lacto-ovo vegetarian. These can be total game-changers in your diet.

If you’re serious about gains, it’s not just about what you eat but also how often you eat.

Double-check that you get enough calories throughout the day to support muscle growth. Keep an eye on your macros — protein, carbs, and fats — because getting the balance right is crucial to maximizing your results.

For optimal muscle growth, it’s not just the total amount of protein you consume daily that matters but also how you distribute it throughout the day. To best support muscle growth and repair, aim to consume protein at each meal and snack, roughly every 3–4 hours. Your initial reference touches on this, but here are some additional resources for more information.

Sure, chicken and rice are out, but who says vegetarian meals have to be boring?

There’s a metric sh*t ton of delicious and protein-packed vegetarian recipes out there. Consider these options:

Not only are these meals muscle-friendly, but they’ll also keep your taste buds happy. Win-win, right?

Sometimes, food alone might not cut it. That’s where supplements come in. There’s strong evidence that creatine supplementation helps with muscle building, and it offers even more benefits for vegan athletes compared to those who eat meat.

Consider adding a high-quality plant-based protein powder to your routine, especially after workouts when your body needs protein the most.

Also, don’t forget about B12 and iron, which can be tricky to get enough of in a vegetarian diet. A good multivitamin can help fill in the gaps.

PSA: It’s important to note that the supplement industry is unregulated. That said, it’s best to recommend third-party verified brands with NSF or Informed Sport certification.

#8760. "Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition

New objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.

Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for new designs: the finds from archaeological digs.

However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.

Deselected finds are duplicates, common in type, poorly preserved or otherwise judged to have limited future research value.

“The material that you see here is the lowest of the lowest quality,” said Isarin at a preview of Ex Situ at this year’s Dutch Design Week. “It’s not preserved. It doesn’t belong in a museum. It doesn’t belong in a depot.”

In fact, if it is not going to be used for educational purposes or reference collections, deselected archaeological finds are required by Dutch law to be carefully destroyed, as they are in many places around the world, said Isarin and Klaster.

Although the materials may be of low value to archaeology, the designers both found this something of a waste. With Ex Situ, they aim to explore a new category of use and preservation for these materials, believing artists and designers have the capacity to tell stories of heritage in a different way to museums.

With the permission of the province of South Holland, they gave deselected materials to nine Dutch practitioners with expertise in crafts such as ceramics, woodwork and glassmaking.

One of the most finished pieces, exhibited in a preview showcase at October’s Dutch Design Week in the Klokgebouw, was by footwear designer and materials researcher Judith Sanders.

She crafted the foundation posts from a section of the Roman Limes border road, dated to 125AD and built under the emperor Hadrian, into the heel of a pair of high-heeled shoes. Sanders was intrigued by the notion that they could perform structurally once again – this time bearing the load of just one person.

Bold numbers on the sides of the shoe denote where on the dig site the material came from, while a second pair of shoes works leather from the middle ages into a modern-day sneaker silhouette.

Another piece is by designer-maker Daan Simons, who worked with 14th-century wood fragments from a ship that was wrecked and then subsequently used in the construction of Rotterdam.

The texture and existing peg holes in the wood are preserved in his Remembrance Pots, which he imagines holding the ashes of a loved one or a keepsake of theirs, compounding the layers of memory in the vessel.

Klaster and Isarin started on the path to Ex Situ after meeting accidentally at their timber drying kiln, where she was having some wood dried for a furniture project, and he was having the deselected Roman posts dried in the hope they would find another life.

“Intrigued by their blackness”, Klaster asked Isarin if she could have them, and went on to make a series of tall vases. That was five years ago, and they have been discussing the potential intersection of archaeology and design ever since.

Klaster says that the Ex Situ designers were supported with information about heritage and the finds they were working with, but that the project naturally inspired some trepidation.

“In the work that they have made so far, you see that they have thought it through, and there is respect in what they made,” said Klaster. “But the first cut with a scissor or a bandsaw is, of course, a scary thing.”

“[One of the designers] was like, can I really saw that in two? And I said yes, you can. If you have a plan as a designer, yes, it’s yours.”

That worry will be echoed among some archaeologists, Isarin adds, and he and Klaster’s aim is for the exhibition to promote discussion among the profession.

“For archaeologists, this material is in a sense sacred,” said Isarin. “But it’s deselected, so nobody wants it.”

He said that while reactions have so far been positive, the issue becomes more thorny if the design were to take place in a commercial context – for instance, if Sanders’ shoes were sold by a fashion brand. In that sense, some archaeologists may see this project as opening a Pandora’s box.

“As soon as we enter the commercial world, then I think for many archaeologists it will be, even though it’s deselected material, an interesting debate ethically,” said Isarin.

“Suppose that all this matter, which has no value at all, that somebody gets rich out of it. That would be a disaster for many archaeologists.”

Nevertheless, Klaster and Isarin think it is a debate worth having.

Pieces in the exhibition come from practitioners ranging from glass artist Bernard Heesen, working with 17th- and 18th-century glass, to conceptual material designer Shahar Livne, working with mammoth bone, and ceramicist Lotte Douwes, working with Roman pottery.

“We have so much rich material beneath our feet, with amazing stories from 40,000 years up to today,” said Klaster.

The exhibition was previewed at Dutch Design Week, alongside the maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive installation by Maison the Faux and Boris Acket and design collective Show Not Show’s Table of Power exhibition.

Ex Situ: Matter in Translation will be on at See Lab, The Hague, from 5 February to 7 March 2027, with discussion events as part of its programming. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

#8759. Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next big thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”

The medication is currently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide users lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

“Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

But, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

If you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more important, he points out.
